note: The (i) beside every page title — SmartPRS 2's screen guide, ported as content. `screens` is keyed by SmartPRS 2's screen id; `routes` maps a SmartPRS 3 route or module key onto one where the names differ (a key that matches needs no line); `fallback` is the guide for a screen nobody has written yet. Entry shape: m module, t title, g tagline, w what it is for, f features [icon,label], s steps, tip, r roles, rel also-see; why/uc/adv are the Why-it-matters tab; mk is Do-it-right [mistake, impact, right way]. Edit the words here, never the PHP.

fallback.w: This screen is part of your SmartPRS workspace. Records you create here follow the same pattern as everywhere else: add or import entries, edit them with the pencil icon, and every change is kept with who made it and when.
s: Use the button at the top right to add a record.
Click Edit on any row to change it.
Use the search box or filters to find records quickly.
fallback.tip: What you can see and change here depends on your role.
fallback.why: Every record kept properly here is a dispute avoided later. Organised, dated, searchable records are what separate a professionally run company from one that runs on memory and WhatsApp forwards.
fallback.uc: Six months from now an auditor, a bank, or an unhappy employee asks "show me the record." You open this screen, filter, and the answer is on the table in thirty seconds.
adv: Zero dependence on anyone's memory
Audit-ready at any moment
New staff learn the process from the screen itself

notifications.g: Every part of your activity stream, explained
notifications.w: This is your own personal activity stream — requests decided, reminders, transfer orders, absence notices — with an unread count against the total, and a note that the bell icon in the top bar is the quick version of this same list. Filter pills across the top (ALL, plus one per notification kind, each with its own count) narrow the list to one type. The table: an unread dot (orange) or read dot (grey), When, Event (a short code), Message (title plus body), For (only visible if you hold audit.tenant.read — who the message was actually for), Channels, State (a badge, e.g. its email delivery status), and per-row actions — an arrow to open whatever screen the notification refers to, and an envelope icon to mark it read without leaving the page. A banner appears if no transport (email/SMS provider) is configured at all, since a queued notification stays queued forever without one; a second banner appears if any stored message still contains something that should have been redacted.
f: The pills across the top filter by notification kind, each showing its own count
The arrow on a row opens the exact screen that notification refers to
The envelope icon marks one notification read without navigating away
The export button (header) downloads the currently filtered list
s: Use the pills to jump straight to one kind of notification (approvals, reminders, transfers, absences).
Click the arrow on any row to go straight to what it's about.
Mark individual items read with the envelope icon, or open them (which also marks them read).
If a banner says nothing has been transmitted, that's a transport (email/SMS) configuration gap, not a bug in this screen — raise it with the dev team rather than expecting messages to arrive.
notifications.tip: Every message here is queued, not necessarily sent — a message only counts as delivered once a transport provider actually acknowledges it, never just because the screen recorded the attempt. That is what the “nothing has been transmitted” banner is warning about when it appears.
r: Everyone (their own notifications); audit.tenant.read adds the ‘For’ column showing who else a message was sent to
notifications.rel: Approvals inbox (header button) — a related but separate list, specifically for approval requests waiting on you.
notifications.why: Treating every message as merely queued until a transport confirms delivery exists to prevent the specific failure of a payroll team believing hundreds of payslip notifications went out when the email gateway silently dropped every one — a status that can only ever say “sent” once something outside this system has actually said so.
notifications.uc: A leave request is approved. The employee whose leave it was gets a new unread notification here (and via the bell) describing the decision, with an arrow straight back to their leave request — they don't have to go hunting for what changed.
adv: One list for every kind of activity notice, filterable by kind rather than scattered across screens
Delivery status is honest about what's merely queued versus provider-confirmed
A stored message flagged as still containing sensitive content is surfaced, not silently kept

att-correction.g: Request a missing check-in or check-out; your approver decides, from a queue across your team
att-correction.w: Reached as “Attendance Regularization” from the menu. A collapsible “Request a regularization” panel at the top holds the raise form: if you can decide requests for others, an “Emp. ID & Name” dropdown picks who it's for (otherwise it's fixed to your own record); a read-only “Shift” line shows the shift that applies (for reference only — it is never checked against what you enter); Check-in Date & Time and Check-out Date & Time (leave either blank if only one punch is missing); a required Reason; and a Request button. A regularization ADDS a punch once approved — the device's own punches are never edited or removed. Below the form, four buttons — Pending / Approved / Rejected / All, each with its own count — filter the queue beneath them. That queue is scoped to your reporting hierarchy: your own requests, anyone who reports to you, anyone whose Team Lead you are, and — for an administrator-tier role — every request in the tenant; nobody sees the whole company's requests just for holding this screen. The table lists, per request: Requested (when it was raised), Employee (linking to their Attendance screen), Day, Check-in asked for, Check-out asked for, Reason, a State badge (amber Pending, green Approved, red Rejected, or purple “mixed” for a legacy pair decided independently before this screen grouped them), Decided (by whom, when, with their note), and — for a pending row, if you can decide — an inline note box plus Approve / Reject buttons right there in the row.
f: “Request a regularization” raises a check-in and/or check-out correction for a missing punch
Pending / Approved / Rejected / All tabs, each showing its own count
Approve or Reject a pending request inline, with an optional note, right from its row
The Employee link on any row opens that person's own Attendance screen
s: Open “Request a regularization”, pick the day, fill in whichever of check-in / check-out is missing, and give a reason.
Submit — the request appears in the Pending queue, scoped to whoever can see it.
Whoever can decide (your manager, HR, or an administrator-tier role) reviews the row and presses Approve or Reject, with an optional note.
Once approved, the missing punch is added to that day's attendance automatically — the original device data is never touched.
att-correction.tip: The Shift shown on the raise form is informational only — it is not validated against the times you enter, so entering a time outside that shift does not block the request.
att-correction.why: A missing punch should never cost an honest employee a day's pay, but letting attendance be edited freely destroys the register's credibility. This screen adds a punch on approval rather than editing an existing one — so the device's own record and the approval trail both survive, and the queue is scoped by the same reporting hierarchy every other screen in the product uses.
att-correction.uc: A device goes offline for a shift and fourteen people show unpaired punches. Each raises one regularization from this screen (or from their own Attendance card); their manager opens the Pending tab, approves them one row at a time with a short note, and the register is right again before payroll runs.
adv: A correction adds a punch — it never edits or erases what the device actually recorded
The queue is scoped to your own reporting hierarchy, never the whole tenant, unless your role is administrator-tier
Every decision keeps who decided it, when, and why
mk: Approving requests without reading the reason
The approval becomes a rubber stamp and the correction trail stops meaning anything
Read the reason on each row before approving — a full day claimed with no punch at all is worth asking about
Leaving requests pending past the payroll cut-off
Payroll runs on attendance that is still wrong, and the correction lands too late to help
Clear the Pending tab before the cut-off, not after

probation.g: Every part of the Probation board, explained
probation.w: The header states the reminder schedule (e.g. “Reminders at 30, 15, 7 days”) and how many reminders were just queued on this visit. The Board groups every employee currently on probation into three badges — overdue (red), due within the configured window (amber), later (grey) — plus a count of anyone with no joining date on file. The table: Code, Name, Department, Designation, Joined, Ends (with an “extended ×N” note if applicable), Days (red if overdue, amber if due soon), State, and two inline actions — Confirm (a date plus remarks, closes probation) and Extend (a new end date plus a required reason). Clicking an employee's code opens their own history card below the board, showing every past confirmation and extension event on their record.
f: Confirm ends probation for that employee as of the date given, with remarks
Extend pushes the end date out, with a mandatory reason — it can be used more than once and each use is counted
“Settings” (header) opens where the probation duration and reminder days are configured
s: Watch the three status badges (overdue / due / later) for a quick sense of who needs a decision.
Use Confirm once probation is genuinely complete, with today's date or the actual confirmation date.
Use Extend, with a reason, if probation needs to run longer — it can be extended more than once.
Click an employee's code to see their full confirmation/extension history.
probation.tip: Confirming probation is recorded as an event on the employee's own timeline, not just a status flag — so the same record used to decide whether a payslip exists also knows exactly when probation ended, which matters for anything statutory that changes at confirmation.
probation.rel: Probation Settings (duration, reminder days) · Directory (the employee list this screen tracks against).
probation.why: A confirmation date recorded as a timeline event, rather than a flag that gets flipped and forgotten, means the exact day probation ended is always answerable later — which matters because statutory applicability (PF, ESI, and similar) can change at confirmation, and a flag alone doesn't say when the flip happened.
probation.uc: An employee's probation is due to end in 7 days. They show up in the amber “due” bucket, and HR either Confirms them (recording the exact date) or Extends with a reason if more time is needed — either way it's a dated, reasoned event on their record, not a silent status change.
adv: Overdue and due-soon employees are surfaced automatically, not something HR has to remember to check
Every confirmation and extension is a dated, reasoned event, kept in full history
Reminders queue automatically at the configured milestones, visible in Notifications

probation-config.g: How long probation runs, and who gets reminded
probation-config.w: Set your company default probation period and the reminder schedule once, and every new joiner follows it automatically. An individual employee can still be given a different period where their role calls for it. You also decide who hears about it: HR, the reporting manager, or both.
f: Default probation months for the company
Notify HR, the manager, or both
Optional congratulations to the employee on confirmation
s: Set the default number of months.
Enter reminder days, e.g. 30, 15, 7, 0.
Choose who should be notified, and save.
probation-config.tip: Reminders are per employee and per milestone, so nobody is spammed even if the sweep runs more than once.
probation-config.why: Policies that live in someone's head get applied inconsistently. Setting the probation period and reminder schedule once means every joiner is treated the same way without anyone having to remember the rule.
probation-config.uc: Picture this: two people join the same week. One is confirmed on time, the other drifts four months because a different manager handled it. One default setting removes that entirely.
adv: Same rule for everyone
Exceptions are deliberate, not accidental
No dependence on any one person's memory

greetings.g: Every part of the Greetings screen, explained
greetings.w: This screen lists every Greeting row in one table, with an Add/Edit form that appears below it on request. The table's columns, left to right, are: Sent at, Target, Recipients, Channels, Message, Sent by, plus Actions. This screen has no search box — the table has no column declared searchable, so every row is always shown. “Add Greeting” (top right, if you hold the edit permission) opens a blank copy of the same form used to Edit; the form's fields are: “Sent at”; “Target”; “Recipients”; “Channels”; “Message”; “Sent by”. Each row's own “Edit” opens that same form pre-filled; “Delete” asks for confirmation first, then retires the row — it stays in history and stops being offered elsewhere in the app, it is not erased outright.
f: “Add Greeting” opens the form below, blank
“Edit” on any row opens the same form, pre-filled with that row
“Delete” retires a row after a confirm prompt — kept in history, not offered elsewhere, never erased outright
s: Click “Add Greeting.”
Fill in whichever of the other fields apply, and Save.
Use Edit to change a row, or Delete to retire it — retiring keeps its history but stops it being offered elsewhere.
greetings.tip: The record count badge above the table and the “page X of Y” note both come from the same underlying count — if a row you expect is missing, check you are not on a later page or mid-search.
greetings.rel: This module's own Add/Edit form is on this same page — there is no separate screen to visit.
greetings.why: Greetings is one of the config-driven modules — its columns and form fields come from config/modules.json, not a hand-written PHP screen, so a customer-specific field never needs a code change (law 1: no business literal in code). The trade-off is that every Greetings row shown here is exactly what that configuration declares, in that order — nothing on this page is hidden logic.
greetings.uc: Example: open “Add Greeting,” fill in Sent at, save, and the new row appears at the top of the table — immediately searchable and immediately available anywhere else in the app that reads this table.
adv: One table and one form for every row — nothing to learn twice
Delete is always a soft retire, never a silent hard delete
The same screen adapts itself the moment the underlying configuration changes

greetings-log.g: Proof of what was actually sent
greetings-log.w: Every greeting that went out, who it was for, and whether the email was delivered. Useful when someone says they never got their birthday wish, and useful for checking that a newly configured message is actually reaching people.
s: Open after the first day greetings are live and confirm messages went out.
If email status shows failed or skipped, check your SMTP settings.
greetings-log.tip: A "skipped" status usually means the employee has no email address on record.
greetings-log.why: Automation you cannot see is automation you cannot trust. The log is how you know the messages are genuinely landing, not silently failing on a bad SMTP setting.
greetings-log.uc: Picture this: greetings have been on for a month. The log shows every message sent — except three staff with no email on record, which is now an easy fix.
adv: Proof the automation is working
Delivery failures surface immediately
Easy to spot missing employee emails

emp-import.g: The three-step wizard, explained step by step
emp-import.w: This is a three-step wizard, each step its own card. “1. Upload”: a file picker for the filled-in bulk upload sample (.xlsx, .xls or .csv), an “If the code already exists” choice (Skip the row, or Update the non-empty cells), and a Preview button; a second “Bulk upload sample” button below it downloads a fresh blank template any time. Once previewed, “2. Preview” appears: a count of rows, how many are ready versus refused, a note naming any uploaded columns nobody captures (ignored, not refused), and a line-by-line table — Line, Code, Name, Action (a green/gray/red badge: create, skip or error), Problems, and Cells (how many values were read for that row). If any row is refused and the import is configured as all-or-nothing, nothing can be imported yet — the button is replaced with a message to fix those rows and re-upload; otherwise “3. Import N row(s)” commits exactly the rows that previewed clean, from the very file just previewed. “History” below lists every past import: When, File, By, Mode, Status, and counts of Rows/Created/Updated/Skipped/Refused.
f: “Bulk upload sample” downloads a blank template with this tenant's own configured employee columns
The file picker plus Preview reads your filled-in sheet without writing anything yet
“Employee fields” (header button) opens the register that defines which columns this import understands
“3. Import N row(s)” commits only the rows that came back clean from the preview — refused rows are never silently written
s: Download “Bulk upload sample” if you don't already have a filled-in sheet.
Fill it in, choose what should happen when a code already exists (Skip or Update), and click Preview.
Read the Preview table — fix any refused (red) rows in the sheet itself, not on this screen, and re-upload if needed.
Once enough rows are ready, click “3. Import N row(s)” to commit exactly what was previewed.
Check History afterwards to confirm the created/updated/skipped/refused counts match what you expected.
emp-import.tip: Columns are matched by the field's own code, its label, or a list of known aliases from other systems (Employee Code, Date of Joining, Mobile No…) — so a reordered sheet, or an export from a different portal, still loads correctly rather than failing on column order.
emp-import.rel: Bulk upload sample and Export all employees on the Directory screen use the same column definition as this import.
emp-import.why: Preview-then-commit off the same file, with an explicit all-or-nothing choice, exists so an import can never leave a staff list half-written from one bad row partway through a large sheet — you see exactly what will happen before anything is saved, and commit reads back the identical file that was previewed, not a second copy of it.
emp-import.uc: A sheet of 40 new joiners has 3 rows with an invalid date format. Preview shows 37 ready and 3 refused with the exact line numbers and problems; with all-or-nothing on, nothing imports until those 3 rows are fixed and the sheet re-uploaded — so the 37 good rows are never risked by importing before the 3 bad ones are caught.
adv: Nothing is written until you explicitly commit a previewed file
Refused rows are named by line and reason, not just counted
Column matching tolerates a reordered sheet or another system's export, by code, label or known alias

absence-config.g: The morning-after check for anyone with no punch and no leave
absence-config.w: Reached as “Absence Alerts” from the menu (route “absence”, titled “Absence sweep” on screen). An expandable “Why the sweep does not decide what absent is” note explains that this screen never runs its own definition of absent — a day is only ever ABSENT because the same published rules the muster and register use said so, so the sweep's mail can never disagree with the payslip the way SmartPRS 2's separate AbsenceService could. A “Settings” card shows an ON/OFF badge and, if you hold tenant.settings.update, three controls: “Sweep enabled”, “Tell the employee”, “Tell the reporting manager (in-app)”, and a Save button; below that, a “Sweep the day” date picker (capped at yesterday) with a “Run now” button re-runs the sweep for one specific day on demand — with the switch off, running it still reports who was absent but notifies nobody. Without update rights, the card just states whether the employee and manager are told. A “Log” table below lists every message the sweep has ever queued: Queued (timestamp), Event, Title, Channels, and a State badge — empty until the sweep has actually run at least once with the switch on and found somebody absent. Messages queue once per employee per day; whether they actually send depends on whether a mail/SMS transport is configured elsewhere — if not, they stay queued and the Notifications screen says so.
f: Sweep enabled — turns the daily absence check on or off entirely
Tell the employee / Tell the reporting manager — independent toggles for who gets notified
“Run now” re-runs the sweep for any one past day on demand, useful for testing or catching up
Log table shows every message the sweep has queued, with its delivery state
s: Turn “Sweep enabled” on, and choose whether to tell the employee, the manager, or both.
Save. From the next morning, anyone with no punch and no approved leave the previous day is queued a message automatically.
Use “Run now” against a specific past date to test the sweep, or to catch a day missed while it was off.
Check the Log to confirm messages are being queued (and, if wired up, actually sent).
absence-config.tip: People on approved leave, holidays and weekly offs are never flagged — the sweep only reaches days the rule engine itself would call ABSENT, the same rules the register and the payslip use.
absence-config.why: SmartPRS 2's absence check re-implemented the same working-days and holiday logic a fourth time, so its mail and the actual payslip could disagree — telling forty people they were absent on a day the register later paid them for, if the device import landed after the mail went out. Reading the same settled-day rules here means the sweep can only ever agree with what payroll will eventually pay.
absence-config.uc: A device goes down overnight. The next morning's sweep queues a message to everyone it affected, each with a link to raise a correction — instead of the gap surfacing three weeks later as a smaller payslip.
adv: The sweep can never disagree with the payslip — both read the same settled-day rules
“Run now” lets a missed or disabled day be caught up on demand, not only at the scheduled hour
Every queued message is logged, so a “did the sweep even run” question has an answer on screen

statutory-config.g: Which signed rate pack is in force for each statutory head today, and where every tenant-editable rule actually lives
statutory-config.w: SmartPRS 2 let an administrator type PF, ESI, PT and TDS rates into a settings row. Here, rates are signed packs under packs/, verified on load — this screen lists which pack is in force for each head today, its version, jurisdiction, and whether it is a real signed pack or a synthetic placeholder ("states no law", shown in red) standing in until a real one is loaded. Below that, it reads three tenant-editable rule files read-only — gratuity.json, statutory-bonus.json, compliance-calendar.json — so you can see exactly what each one currently declares without opening the file yourself. The three older SmartPRS 2 settings screens (PF & ESI, TDS rules, PT slabs) still exist as reference-data registers, linked from here, until packs carry them too.
f: Rate packs in force today, per statutory head, with version and jurisdiction
A synthetic pack (no real law behind it yet) is flagged red, never shown as if it were signed
Read-only view of gratuity.json, statutory-bonus.json and compliance-calendar.json as they stand
Links to the reference-data registers (PF & ESI, TDS rules, PT slabs) not yet carried by a pack
s: Open Statutory Configuration to see which rate pack is actually deciding a figure today, and whether it is signed or synthetic.
Use the read-only file views to check a rule (an eligibility ceiling, a due-date window) without needing repository access.
If payroll closes without statutory lines, check here first — a missing or unavailable pack is stated plainly.
statutory-config.tip: A red "synthetic — states no law" badge is not an error to fix in this screen — it means no real signed pack has been loaded for that head yet, and payroll will say so on every affected payslip until one is.
statutory-config.rel: Also see: Gratuity, Statutory Bonus, TDS, PF & ESI
statutory-config.why: A rate typed into a settings row is a number attributed to nobody, that somebody eventually deducts from a real salary. A signed pack has a named compliance owner and a version, so a rate change is a traceable event, not an edit that quietly changes what people are paid.
statutory-config.uc: Picture this: a payslip shows no PF line and nobody knows why. You open Statutory Configuration, see PF has no pack in force, and now know exactly what has to be loaded before payroll can compute it — rather than guessing at a bug.
adv: No statutory rate is ever a PHP literal — every one traces to a signed, versioned pack
A synthetic (not-yet-real) pack is visibly flagged, so a placeholder can never be mistaken for a law
The tenant's own editable rules are one screen away, read-only here and edited on their own dedicated screens

dashboard.w: The dashboard shows the health of your workforce right now — active employees, who is present today, approvals waiting for you, compliance flags and the latest payroll. Every number is live and clickable.
s: Check the cards each morning — they answer "is anything waiting for me?"
Click any card to jump straight to that screen.
Use the company switcher in the top bar to see one company or the whole group.
dashboard.tip: The Live Salary card at the bottom shows YOUR OWN salary earned till today — every employee sees their own.
r: Everyone — numbers scoped to your role
dashboard.rel: Also see: Live Salary, Approvals Inbox
dashboard.why: A business you cannot see, you cannot run. The dashboard exists so the owner's first minute of the day answers the only question that matters: is anything on fire?
dashboard.uc: Picture this: 9:05 AM, you open SmartPRS with your chai. 4 absent in the Hyderabad branch, 2 approvals waiting, 1 DRA expiring this month. Three phone calls before 9:30 and the day is already under control.
adv: Problems surface before they grow
No more "sir, I didn't know" — everyone sees the same truth
Management by numbers, not by mood

live-salary.g: Salary earned till today, entry by entry
live-salary.w: Instead of waiting for month-end, this screen shows how much salary has been earned up to today — basic, allowances, deductions, plus approved overtime, loan EMIs, advance recoveries and every commission entry, including ones still awaiting approval. It uses the same engine (and the same Salary/LOP day basis setting) as the real payroll, so the numbers always match.
s: Open the screen — your own live salary loads automatically.
Switch to the Commissions & Incentives tab to see every entry and whether it is approved, pending or locked.
Managers and HR can pick any team member from the dropdown.
live-salary.tip: Pending commissions are shown but NOT counted in the big number until approved — the amber chip tells you what is awaiting approval. Curious what next month could look like with more collections or overtime? The Simulator button opens a what-if payslip where you can change every variable.
live-salary.rel: Also see: Commission Entries, Salary & Commission Ledger
live-salary.why: In collections, the #1 reason agents quit or argue is "salary ka hisaab clear nahi hai." Live Salary kills that argument by showing every employee their money, building up daily, entry by entry.
live-salary.uc: Picture this: your agent collects ₹40,000 on Tuesday and his incentive entry is approved Wednesday. He opens Live Salary and SEES it sitting in his month — he doesn't call HR, he goes and collects more.
adv: Salary disputes drop to near zero
Motivation: agents watch their earnings grow daily
HR stops answering "mera kitna bana?" twenty times a day

escalations.g: Two things on one page: the field/ops incident register, and approval SLA breaches
escalations.w: “Add Escalation” logs a field/ops incident: Date, Company, Bank, Team, Issue (a free-text description), Severity, Priority, Status and Action taken — all from configured option lists. The table below lists every logged incident with the same fields, each row editable inline (Status plus Action taken, with an Update button) without opening a separate form. Further down, an entirely separate section, “Approvals past their due-within,” is an SLA dashboard for the whole product's approval workflows (not just escalations): four tiles — breached, within due-within, no deadline declared, open in all — then a Breached table (which approval step, who it's waiting on, how overdue, how many of the people who could act on it actually have a linked login) with an Escalate action per row (or Escalate all at once), and a shorter Within due-within table for steps still on track.
f: “Add Escalation” logs one field/ops incident against a bank, team and issue
The inline Status/Action taken update on the incident table saves without opening a separate form
“Escalate” (or “Escalate all”) on a breached approval step notifies whoever holds the role it's waiting on
“All requests” (header) opens the full approvals inbox, beyond just breached items
s: Use Add Escalation to log a new field/ops incident as it happens.
Update Status and Action taken inline on the register as an incident progresses.
Check the SLA tiles further down for any approval step that's breached its due-within — unrelated to the incident register above it.
Escalate a breached step (or all of them) to notify the people who can actually act on it.
escalations.tip: The escalation register (top) and the approval-SLA dashboard (bottom) are two different systems sharing one page — a breach in the SLA section is about an approval step waiting too long somewhere else in the product, not about anything typed into the incident register above it.
escalations.rel: All requests (the full approvals inbox, header button) shows every approval, not just the breached ones.
escalations.why: Breach time is fixed to the deadline itself, not to when somebody happened to look — so a step already overdue when this screen is opened shows as breached immediately, rather than only once someone manually notices and marks it late.
escalations.uc: A leave approval has sat with a branch manager for three days past its due-within. It appears in the Breached table naming the exact step, who it's waiting on, and how many of that role's holders actually have a linked login to be notified — clicking Escalate queues them a notification directly.
adv: Field/ops incidents can be updated inline without opening a separate edit screen
Breach detection is based on the deadline itself, never on someone remembering to check
Escalating shows exactly who is reachable (has a linked login) versus who would need to be told another way

approvals-inbox.w: One inbox for every request where you are the approver — leave, expenses, advances, loans, commissions, increments, transfers and more. Decide from here without hunting through each module.
f: All pending requests in one list
Tap a name for the profile card
s: Open the inbox — newest requests are on top.
Click a row to see the full details.
Approve or reject; add remarks so the employee knows why.
approvals-inbox.tip: The bell icon in the top bar shows the same count — it updates live as requests arrive.
r: Anyone who approves — managers, HR, Admin
approvals-inbox.why: Approvals delayed are trust destroyed — an employee waiting five days for a ₹500 expense learns his company doesn't care. One inbox makes deciding so easy there is no excuse to delay.
approvals-inbox.uc: Picture this: a team leader opens one screen with morning tea, clears six requests in four minutes, and every one of those six employees starts the day feeling heard.
adv: Decisions in minutes, not days
Nothing waits in a forgotten email
Employees trust a system that responds

how-it-works.w: A guided overview of how the pieces fit together — how attendance flows into payroll, how approvals move, and where to start as a new user.
s: Read top to bottom once when you join.
Come back whenever a flow feels unclear.
how-it-works.tip: Every screen also has this ⓘ guide — tap it anywhere you feel lost.
how-it-works.why: Training time is money. This orientation exists so a new user becomes productive in their first hour, without a trainer sitting beside them.
how-it-works.uc: Picture this: you hire a new HR executive Monday. By lunch, she has read this once, used the ⓘ on three screens, and processed her first leave request — zero training calls to you.
adv: New staff productive on day one
No dependence on one "system expert"
Self-service reduces your training cost to zero

kb.g: Every part of the Knowledge base screen, explained
kb.w: This screen lists every Knowledge base row in one table, with an Add/Edit form that appears below it on request. The table's columns, left to right, are: Title, Category, Icon, Body, Roles, Sort, plus Actions. “Title” carries a small coloured initials avatar, since it is the column that names the row. The search box above the table searches only title — typing there and pressing Search (or clearing it with the Clear link) is the only filter this screen has. “Add Knowledge base” (top right, if you hold the edit permission) opens a blank copy of the same form used to Edit; the form's fields are: “Title” (required); “Category”; “Icon”; “Body”; “Roles”. Structured data. A list looks like ["one","two"]; a setting like {"key":"value"}.; “Sort”. Each row's own “Edit” opens that same form pre-filled; “Delete” asks for confirmation first, then retires the row — it stays in history and stops being offered elsewhere in the app, it is not erased outright.
f: “Add Knowledge base” opens the form below, blank
Search box filters the table by title; Clear resets it
“Edit” on any row opens the same form, pre-filled with that row
“Delete” retires a row after a confirm prompt — kept in history, not offered elsewhere, never erased outright
s: Click “Add Knowledge base.”
Fill in the required field(s): Title.
Fill in whichever of the other fields apply, and Save.
Later, use Search (over title) to find the row again.
Use Edit to change a row, or Delete to retire it — retiring keeps its history but stops it being offered elsewhere.
kb.tip: The record count badge above the table and the “page X of Y” note both come from the same underlying count — if a row you expect is missing, check you are not on a later page or mid-search.
kb.rel: This module's own Add/Edit form is on this same page — there is no separate screen to visit.
kb.why: Knowledge base is one of the config-driven modules — its columns and form fields come from config/modules.json, not a hand-written PHP screen, so a customer-specific field never needs a code change (law 1: no business literal in code). The trade-off is that every Knowledge base row shown here is exactly what that configuration declares, in that order — nothing on this page is hidden logic.
kb.uc: Example: open “Add Knowledge base,” fill in Title, save, and the new row appears at the top of the table — immediately searchable by title and immediately available anywhere else in the app that reads this table.
adv: One table and one form for every row — nothing to learn twice
Delete is always a soft retire, never a silent hard delete
The same screen adapts itself the moment the underlying configuration changes

emp-list.g: Every part of the Directory screen, explained
emp-list.w: This is the main Employee Directory (the same screen also serves “Archived” — employees who have exited or been archived — and “Me” — your own linked profile, filtered to one row). At the top: the standard Company/Branch/Department/Designation/Role/Team filter bar, then three stat tiles — Employees on file, Contracted gross per month (shown as a lock icon instead of a figure if you don't hold employee.salary.view — an aggregate total is still salary data), and Departments named. The header buttons are Export all employees (downloads every visible row as a file), Bulk upload sample (downloads a blank template with exactly this tenant's configured columns), Import Employee (goes to the bulk-import screen, which reads that same template back in), and Add New Employee (opens the add form further down the page, not a separate screen). The table itself is dynamic: it always shows every employee field this tenant has actually configured under Employee Fields Register, not a fixed list — so a tenant that tracks a UAN, a shift or a mother's name sees that column here without anyone building it in, and the table scrolls sideways rather than hiding a configured field. Name, code and photo (if the photo field is enabled) lead each row; documents on file for that employee are indicated per row, though the document itself opens only for someone holding employee.document.view.
f: “Export all employees” downloads every row currently matching the filter bar
“Bulk upload sample” downloads a blank template with this tenant's own configured columns — exported and imported columns always match
“Import Employee” opens the bulk-import screen that reads that template back in
“Add New Employee” jumps down to the add form on this same page, rather than a separate screen
The Contracted gross tile shows a lock icon instead of a number for anyone without employee.salary.view — an aggregate is still salary data
s: Use the filter bar to narrow the directory to one company, branch, department, designation, role or team.
Read the three stat tiles for a quick headcount / payroll-cost / department-count summary of exactly what's filtered in.
Scroll the table sideways to see every field this tenant has configured — nothing configured is hidden off-screen permanently.
Use Add New Employee to add one person, or Bulk upload sample → fill it in → Import Employee to add many at once.
Use Export all employees any time you need the current filtered view as a file outside the app.
emp-list.tip: The bulk upload sample and the Import Employee screen are deliberately built from the same column set as the directory table — a file that came out of Export or the sample always has the columns Import Employee expects back.
emp-list.rel: Add New Employee (same page, further down) · Import Employee · Archived (this same screen, filtered) · Me (this same screen, showing only your own linked profile).
emp-list.why: The employee table's columns are configuration (Employee Fields Register), not a fixed schema — so this directory is built to always reflect whatever fields this specific tenant actually captures, rather than a generic HR system's idea of what an employee record should contain. That is also why the export/import/sample all share one column definition: a customisation to the fields register changes all three at once, never just one of them.
emp-list.uc: A tenant adds a custom “Vehicle Number” field for field-force employees under Employee Fields Register. The very next time this Directory, its Export, its Bulk upload sample, and Import Employee are opened, Vehicle Number is already there — no code change, no separate template to update by hand.
adv: Every configured employee field shows up here automatically — nothing to separately wire in per field
Export, sample and import always share one column definition, so a round trip through the three never mismatches
A payroll-cost total is gated the same way an individual salary is — an aggregate is still salary data

teams.g: Every part of the Teams screen, explained
teams.w: “Add Team” opens a dialog: Team Name, Function, Company, Status, Manager (only employees holding a ‘manager’ designation are offered), and Team Leader (only those holding ‘team leader’). The main table: Team Name, Function, Company, Manager, Team Leader, Members (a count, clickable to expand the actual member list inline), Under TL (everyone reporting to that team's leader, a different count from Members), Status, and Edit/Delete. Membership is derived, not assigned here: an employee belongs to a team because their own employee record names that team (by team_id or by typing the team's name) — there is no separate “add member” step on this screen. Deleting a team retires it; employees keep their own records and simply stop showing a team.
f: “Add Team” creates a team shell — name, function, company, manager, leader
Edit changes a team's own details, never its membership
Delete retires a team — member employee records are untouched, they simply stop naming an active team
The Members count expands inline to the actual list of employees whose record names this team
s: Click Add Team and fill in its name, function, company, manager and team leader.
To add or remove a member, edit that person's own employee record and change their Team field — not this screen.
Click a team's Members or Under TL count to see exactly who that number refers to, without leaving the page.
Delete a team only once nobody needs it any more — members are unaffected but stop showing that team.
teams.tip: Members and Under TL are two different counts on purpose: Members is who names this team on their own record; Under TL is everyone reporting to the team's designated leader — the two overlap in a well-organised team but are not guaranteed to match.
teams.rel: An employee's own record (Directory → Edit) is where team membership is actually set.
teams.why: Deriving membership from the employee's own record, rather than a separate membership list here, means a team can never quietly disagree with what the Directory says about who's on it — there is exactly one place that fact lives.
teams.uc: A new collections team is created for a new city. Add Team names it, sets its manager and leader; as each new hire's employee record is set to that team, they appear in this screen's Members list automatically — with no separate step to add them here.
adv: Membership can never drift from the employee record, because there's only one place it's stored
Manager and Team Leader dropdowns are pre-filtered to people who actually hold those designations
Deleting a team is safe for its members' own records — nothing about them is deleted

idcard.g: Every part of this screen, explained
idcard.w: An Employee dropdown (“— pick to preview a card —”, jump-to-select, no separate Go button) is the whole entry point; picking a name immediately renders that person's card below using the same org filter bar (Company/Branch/Department/Designation/Role/Team) shown while nobody is picked yet. The rendered card shows every value straight from the employee record — name, code, designation, photo, company logo — in whichever ID Card Format currently applies to that person, resolved by the same most-specific-wins ladder as Salary Structure (their own record beats their designation, which beats their department, branch, then company). Beside the card: “Print ID Card PDF”, and a note naming which named format matched (or “Default format” if none did), the card's physical size and orientation in millimetres, and a reminder that a wrong designation or photo is fixed on the employee record itself, never on this screen. Two header buttons: “ID Card Format” (goes to the separate screen where card layouts and their scopes are designed) and “Directory” (back to the employee list).
f: The Employee dropdown previews any one person's card instantly, without a separate submit
“Print ID Card PDF” generates the exact card shown, embedding the actual photo and company logo files on record
“ID Card Format” (header) opens the separate screen that designs card layouts and decides which scope each one applies to
s: Pick an employee from the dropdown — their card renders immediately below.
Check the note beside the card for which named format matched and its physical size.
Click “Print ID Card PDF” to generate the printable file.
If a detail on the card is wrong, fix it on the employee's own record — this screen only ever displays what's already there.
To change how cards look (not whose data they show), go to ID Card Format and design or rescope a layout.
idcard.tip: A card's format is resolved per employee — their own record's format wins over their designation's, which wins over their department's, branch's, then company's. If a card looks wrong for one person only, check whether a format was scoped directly to them before assuming the tenant-wide format is broken.
idcard.rel: ID Card Format (layout design, separate screen) · Directory (the employee list this screen picks from).
idcard.why: A printed card that fell out of sync with the employee record is worse than no card — someone carries a badge with an old designation. Reading every value live from the record, rather than storing a snapshot at print time, means the card is always correct as of the moment it's printed, and the fix for a wrong card is always the same one fix: correct the record.
idcard.uc: A field agent is promoted from Executive to Team Lead. Their designation is updated once on their employee record; the very next time anyone opens ID Cards for them, the card already shows Team Lead — and if Team Lead has its own scoped card format (a different colour band, say), that format applies automatically too, with no separate step.
adv: A card can never drift from the employee record it represents — there is no separate stored snapshot to fall out of date
Format resolution follows the same most-specific-wins scope logic used elsewhere in the product, so it behaves predictably
The exact physical size and orientation are stated beside every preview, before printing

transfers.g: Every part of the Transfers workflow, explained
transfers.w: “Raise Transfer” opens a dialog to start a branch, department or company move: employee, type, destination, effective date, and reason. The table: a status badge per row (pending, approved, applied, rejected), and every raised transfer with its type and destination. Once approved, an order letter (from the ‘transfer’ HR Letters template) is generated automatically and queued to the employee as a notification with an acknowledgement link — the employee (or an HR user on their behalf) reads the order on this same screen and clicks “I acknowledge this transfer order,” which records receipt on their file without changing the move itself. The move actually takes effect on the effective date, written to the employee's own timeline, keeping the same employee code across companies.
f: “Raise Transfer” starts a move — type, destination, effective date, reason
The order preview can be printed or saved as a PDF directly from this screen
“I acknowledge this transfer order” records the employee's receipt of the order, separate from approving or applying the move itself
The export button (header) downloads the current filtered list
s: Click Raise Transfer, fill in the employee, move type, destination, effective date and reason.
Have someone else (not the person who raised it) approve the transfer.
Once approved, the order letter is generated and queued to the employee automatically — no separate step to send it.
The employee (or HR for them) opens the order and acknowledges it on this screen.
The move applies itself on the effective date, recorded on the employee's timeline.
transfers.tip: Acknowledging an order records receipt — it does not itself approve or apply the transfer. The move happens on its own effective date regardless of whether it's been acknowledged, so an unacknowledged order is worth following up on, not treated as a blocked move.
transfers.rel: HR Letters (the ‘transfer’ template used for the order) · Notifications (where the queued order link appears for the employee).
transfers.why: A move with a paper trail — raised by one person, approved by another, an order letter issued automatically, and an acknowledgement recorded — is what keeps a branch or company transfer from being a verbal instruction nobody can later point to. The same employee code carrying across companies is what keeps their history in one place through the move.
transfers.uc: An employee moves from the Hyderabad branch to the Pune branch. The transfer is raised, approved by their manager's manager (not the same person who raised it), the order letter goes out automatically, the employee acknowledges it from the link in their Notifications, and on the effective date their record shows Pune — with their full attendance and payroll history intact under the same employee code.
adv: The order letter is generated and queued automatically on approval — no separate step to draft or send it
Acknowledgement and approval are two distinct, separately recorded facts
The employee keeps one continuous history across the move, under one code

documents.g: Every part of the Document Tracker, explained
documents.w: The header line states four live counts: documents on file, employees they cover, how many are expired or expiring within the configured window, and how many employees are missing an expected document — plus the allowed file types and max size per file. A red banner names the first several expiring/expired documents directly (employee, kind, expiry date) when any exist. “Add Document” opens a dialog: Employee, Document Kind (free text with suggestions from what Employee fields already expects), Expiry date, File, and Status. Below, a filter bar plus a search box (by employee name or ID) and a “Show who is missing an expected document” checkbox. The main table is one row per employee: Employee (with department/branch beneath), Documents (a count plus a breakdown by kind, e.g. “PAN, Aadhaar (2)”), Soonest expiry (a green/amber/red badge), Missing (green “complete” or a red count naming which kinds), and an eye icon that expands that row into its own document list — Kind, File (a link, or a red “no file” badge), Status (editable inline if you may edit), Expiry, Added, and a per-document Delete (kept in history, not destroyed).
f: “Add Document” uploads one document for one employee, with an optional expiry date
The search box filters the employee rows by name or ID
The eye icon on a row expands that employee's full document list in place, without leaving the page
The small + icon on a row opens Add Document pre-filled for that employee
The inline Status/Expiry save on an expanded document updates that one document without a page reload
Delete removes one document — kept in history, not destroyed
s: Tick “Show who is missing an expected document” to see gaps against what Employee fields declares should be on file.
Use the search box or the filter bar to narrow to one employee, branch or department.
Click the eye icon on a row to see (or add to) that employee's actual documents.
Watch the expiring/expired banner at the top — it lists specific employees and kinds, not just a count.
Update a document's Status or Expiry inline once it's expanded, or delete it if it was added in error.
documents.tip: “Missing” is worked out against the document kinds Employee fields expects for this tenant, not a hardcoded list — what counts as a gap here changes automatically if that configuration changes.
documents.rel: Expected document kinds come from Organization Setup → Employee fields.
documents.why: A document that quietly expires with nobody noticing is the whole risk this screen exists to remove — so expiring and expired documents are surfaced by name in a banner at the top, not buried in a status column somebody has to think to check, and “missing” is computed against configuration rather than being a manually maintained checklist that drifts.
documents.uc: An employee's police verification is due to expire in 20 days and the tracking window is 30 days. It shows up in the red banner at the top by name and kind the moment the screen opens — nobody has to search for it or remember to check.
adv: Expiring and expired documents are named up front, not just counted
Missing-document gaps are computed against the same configuration Employee fields already declares
A document's status can be updated without leaving the tracker or losing your place in a long employee list

bgv.g: The desk screen, plus the plain register behind it
bgv.w: The header states live counts: records, plus how many are clear / discrepancy / in progress / pending, and the re-verification window (amber within N days, red past due). A filter bar narrows by the usual org fields; “Start a verification for…” (a dropdown of employees with none yet, plus Add) begins one. The main table is one row per employee — name, department/branch beneath — clicking a row opens its own card: an overall status badge and a form with one dropdown per check (Identity/KYC, Address, Education, Employment, Criminal, References — each clear/flag/na/pending), an Agency field, Completed on, Verified on, Re-verify every (months), and the resulting Next due date. A “Register” button in the header opens the plain generic table view of the same underlying data (Employee, Overall Status, Completed on, Agency, per-check columns, Verified On, Next Re-verify Due) with ordinary Add/Edit/Delete — useful for a raw list or bulk edit, but the desk view above is where the actual per-check outcomes are recorded and read day to day.
f: “Start a verification for…” begins a record for an employee who doesn't have one yet
Clicking an employee's row opens their own outcomes form — six checks, each its own status
“Register” (header) opens the plain Add/Edit/Delete table behind this desk view
Overdue re-verification dates render in red; due-soon in amber — both computed from the configured window
s: Use “Start a verification for…” to begin tracking a new employee.
Open their row and set each of the six checks as they come back — clear, flag, not applicable, or still pending.
Set Verified on and Re-verify every (months) once the overall check is done — Next due is worked out from those.
Watch the header counts and the due-date colours to see who needs attention without opening every row.
Use Register only when you need the plain table view — the desk view above it is where checks are actually recorded.
bgv.tip: Overall status is derived from the six individual checks, not set directly — if a record won't show “clear”, check whether every one of the six checks (not just the ones you touched) is actually marked clear.
bgv.rel: Register (same data, plain Add/Edit/Delete table) is one button away from the desk view.
bgv.why: Six separate checks (identity, address, education, employment, criminal, references) collapsed into one desk view, rather than six columns in a generic table, is what makes it obvious at a glance which specific check is still open for a given employee — a single “status” column can't show that.
bgv.uc: A re-verification is due in 12 days and the window is set to 30. It shows amber in both the header count and that employee's Next Re-verify Due, so HR can act before it lapses into red (past due) rather than discovering it after the fact.
adv: Six independent checks stay visible as six checks, not folded into one ambiguous status
Due dates are colour-coded automatically from the configured re-verification window
The plain register is still there for a raw list or bulk edit, one click away

onboarding-board.g: The new-joiner checklist board, the invite-and-verify console, and the joiner's own form
onboarding-board.w: This one help key covers four different screens. The one you reach from the People menu — route “Onboarding” — is a checklist board: the header line shows how many boards exist and how many are Pending / In progress / Completed, with an org filter bar and a row of status pills (All, Pending, In progress, Completed, each showing its own count) that re-filter the board by clicking. If any employee has no board yet, a “Start onboarding for” row appears above the cards with an employee dropdown, a Checklist dropdown (the named lists in config/onboarding.json, each shown with its item count) and a Start button; a “Start for recent joiners” button in the header does the same in bulk for everyone hired in the configured window. Each employee gets one card: their name (linking to their employee record), a status badge, a purple “Transfer” badge if this checklist was started because they transferred in rather than joined fresh, the stage name, joined-on date, a “X of Y done” count, and a progress bar (orange until 100%, then green). Below that is a grid of buttons, one per checklist item — Documents, ID card, system access, training, whatever that checklist names — each toggling between an empty square and a green checked square on click; ticking the last item completes the card automatically, no separate “mark complete” step exists. Under the grid, three links jump straight to that person's other setup: “Assign role, manager & team” (opens their employee record), “ID card”, and “Background verification.” A “Self-Onboarding” button in the header opens the second screen this key covers: the Verification Console, where you invite a joiner by name/email/mobile (or pick “existing” to redo onboarding for someone already on file), or bulk-invite from a CSV of name/email/mobile. No email or SMS sender is wired up in this build, so the invite link is shown on screen for you to copy and send yourself — it opens with no login, stays open for the configured number of days, and shows the joiner only the fields ticked on under Employee Fields. A left-hand list of submissions (filterable by Invited / Draft / Submitted / Correction / Injected / Disabled) opens, on the right, a field-by-field review table with a Verified checkbox per field; a Submitted case gets a “Request correction” box (free text the joiner will see) and an “Approve” box, which — for a brand-new joiner — first asks for the real employee code, CTC and date of joining plus any HR-only fields (reporting line, cost code, statutory and pay settings) the joiner was never shown, then creates the employee record once “I have verified the submitted fields” is ticked. If you reach the same route without permission to create employees, you instead see the third screen: “Complete your details” — your own cut-down version of the same form (no employee code, CTC, status or commission fields), for filling in your own record. There is also a plain register, “Onboarding Tracker” (reached via Customise → the generic module table, not from this board), which tracks recruitment-pipeline stages — Offer accepted, Documents pending, Documents verified, Background check, Ready to join, Joined, Dropped — as a separate Add/Edit/Delete table, independent of the checklist boards above. Finally, the link a joiner receives opens a fifth, completely separate page with no menu, sidebar or Screen Guide at all — just their own name, a progress bar, the fields and document-upload slots HR enabled, and “Save and continue later” / “Submit to HR” buttons; a wrong or expired link shows “This link does not open” and nothing else.
f: “Start for recent joiners” starts a board for everyone hired inside the configured window, in one click
Click any checklist-item button to tick or untick it — the card's progress bar and status update immediately
“Assign role, manager & team”, “ID card” and “Background verification” jump straight to that person's other onboarding steps
Self-Onboarding: “+ Invite” (or bulk CSV import) generates a no-login link for the joiner to fill in themselves
Self-Onboarding: tick each submitted field “Verified” before Approve is meaningful — Approve does not check this for you
Self-Onboarding “Approve” creates the employee record (or updates an existing one) from the joiner's own submission
s: From the People menu, open Onboarding to see every board, or click Self-Onboarding to invite a joiner to fill in their own details first.
On the board: use “Start onboarding for” (or “Start for recent joiners”) to create a checklist card for someone who doesn't have one yet.
Tick items off on their card as each is actually done — documents received, ID card printed, access granted, training booked.
In Self-Onboarding: send the shown link to the joiner, then once they submit, open their row, tick each field Verified, and either Approve (to inject them as an employee) or Request correction.
Use “Assign role, manager & team”, “ID card” and “Background verification” from the card to finish the steps this board doesn't do itself.
onboarding-board.tip: A checklist completes itself the moment its last item is ticked — there is no separate “mark complete” button, and nothing stops you ticking items out of order if the real-world work happened out of order.
onboarding-board.rel: Also see: Employees, Employee Fields, ID Cards, Background Verification, Transfers, Recruitment
onboarding-board.why: A joiner who waits days for system access or an ID card starts on the back foot. Splitting this into a checklist board (what still needs doing) and a self-onboarding console (getting the joiner's own details without HR retyping them) means nothing depends on one person remembering every step, and the fields a joiner is asked for are exactly the ones Employee Fields has switched on — never a second, drifting list.
onboarding-board.uc: A candidate accepts an offer on Friday. HR sends them the self-onboarding link over the weekend; by Monday morning their documents and personal details are sitting in the Verification Console, HR ticks each field verified, sets the real employee code and CTC, and approves — the employee record and their onboarding checklist board both exist before they've had their first coffee on site.
adv: The joiner types their own details once, into fields HR already chose to collect — nobody retypes a form
A checklist card makes “is this person actually ready” a glance, not a memory test
Approve requires an explicit “I have verified” tick — nothing gets injected as an employee unread
mk: HR retypes what the joiner emailed on a PDF form
Typos, mismatched values, and the joiner's original answer is lost
Send the Self-Onboarding link instead — the joiner's own typing becomes the record once approved
A checklist item gets ticked before the real-world step happened
The board reports someone ready who isn't, and nobody double-checks
Tick items only once the work is actually done — the board has no way to tell the difference
Approving a submission without ticking any field Verified
An unverified detail (a misspelled name, a wrong PAN) becomes the permanent employee record
Tick Verified per field as you actually check it, not as a formality before Approve

recruitment.g: Portal data to hired — at volume
recruitment.w: Your complete hiring desk: raise requisitions with approval, import hundreds of candidates from job portals into the Talent Pool, send bulk WhatsApp interview or walk-in invites, run Hiring Drives, interview with panel scores, and convert to employee in one click.
s: Raise a requisition for the position; an admin approves it.
Import the job-portal export (Excel/CSV) into the Talent Pool and filter to the matching candidates.
Shortlist and send a bulk WhatsApp invite — or plan a Hiring Drive with venue, map link and panel.
Mark attendance and scores during interviews; hit Hire on the selected ones.
The hire becomes a full employee with onboarding started automatically.
recruitment.tip: Every bulk send becomes a tracked campaign under the WhatsApp Campaigns tab — sent, delivered, interested, attended, hired. And during the interview itself, click the Salary Simulator button (top of this screen) — enter the offer CTC and show the candidate a live payslip illustration of their exact in-hand, with PF, ESI, PT and TDS worked out. Print it as a one-page handout.
recruitment.why: Collections is a volume-hiring business — agents churn, portfolios grow, and the agency that hires fastest serves the bank best. This screen turns hiring from a phone-call grind into an assembly line.
recruitment.uc: Picture this: Naukri gives you 300 CVs Monday morning. By 11 AM they're imported, filtered to 120, and a walk-in invite with the map link is on every WhatsApp. Thursday you hire 14 — without making one phone call.
adv: Days of calling become one bulk WhatsApp
Every candidate tracked — none lost in Excel
Hiring speed becomes your sales pitch to banks
mk: Sending bulk WhatsApp before the template is approved
Every message fails; candidates get nothing and you wait another day
Check WhatsApp Templates first — the row must show green APPROVED; a test send proves it
Importing portal files without a mobile column
Candidates land in the pool but can't be invited — the whole point is lost
Use the template or keep portal exports' mobile column intact; check the import summary
Hiring without linking a requisition
Openings never show as filled; you over-hire without noticing
Always attach candidates to an approved requisition; the fill-count then manages itself

offroll-agents.g: Every part of the Off-roll agents screen, explained
offroll-agents.w: This screen lists every Off-roll agent row in one table, with an Add/Edit form that appears below it on request. The table's columns, left to right, are: Name, Mobile, Status, plus Actions. “Name” carries a small coloured initials avatar, since it is the column that names the row. Status render as a coloured status badge, not plain text. The search box above the table searches only name, mobile — typing there and pressing Search (or clearing it with the Clear link) is the only filter this screen has. “Add Off-roll agent” (top right, if you hold the edit permission) opens a blank copy of the same form used to Edit; the form's fields are: “Name” (required); “Mobile”; “Status” — a dropdown: Onboarded, Active, Suspended, Terminated. Each row's own “Edit” opens that same form pre-filled; “Delete” asks for confirmation first, then retires the row — it stays in history and stops being offered elsewhere in the app, it is not erased outright.
f: “Add Off-roll agent” opens the form below, blank
Search box filters the table by name, mobile; Clear resets it
“Edit” on any row opens the same form, pre-filled with that row
“Delete” retires a row after a confirm prompt — kept in history, not offered elsewhere, never erased outright
s: Click “Add Off-roll agent.”
Fill in the required field(s): Name.
Fill in whichever of the other fields apply, and Save.
Later, use Search (over name, mobile) to find the row again.
Use Edit to change a row, or Delete to retire it — retiring keeps its history but stops it being offered elsewhere.
offroll-agents.tip: The record count badge above the table and the “page X of Y” note both come from the same underlying count — if a row you expect is missing, check you are not on a later page or mid-search.
offroll-agents.rel: This module's own Add/Edit form is on this same page — there is no separate screen to visit.
offroll-agents.why: Off-roll agents is one of the config-driven modules — its columns and form fields come from config/modules.json, not a hand-written PHP screen, so a customer-specific field never needs a code change (law 1: no business literal in code). The trade-off is that every Off-roll agents row shown here is exactly what that configuration declares, in that order — nothing on this page is hidden logic.
offroll-agents.uc: Example: open “Add Off-roll agent,” fill in Name, save, and the new row appears at the top of the table — immediately searchable by name and immediately available anywhere else in the app that reads this table.
adv: One table and one form for every row — nothing to learn twice
Delete is always a soft retire, never a silent hard delete
The same screen adapts itself the moment the underlying configuration changes

att-daily.g: One employee, every settled day, and why each one was called that
att-daily.w: This is the per-employee attendance screen (menu item “Attendance”, reached directly, or from a row's own “Attendance” link elsewhere). An “Employee” dropdown plus “Shift starts” / “Shift ends” override fields and a Settle button choose who and which shift window to read — set the end earlier than the start (22:00 to 06:00) to fold an overnight shift into one attendance day, labelled by the date it started. Nothing on this screen is stored: every figure is derived from the raw punches on read, so a corrected punch changes the payslip without a job to re-run. Once an employee is picked, three stat cards show Days settled, Payable days, and Needing attention (red once above zero). If you hold manual-punch rights, a “Record a punch” form (When, Direction In/Out, Record) adds one instantly. The “Settled days” table lists, per day: the date (with a purple “crosses midnight, ONE day” badge where that applied), a Status badge (Present / Half day / Absent / Unclassified, coloured, with the rule's own explanation on hover and the rule code printed under it), Worked/Late/Early exit/Overtime/Shortfall in minutes, and Flags — “needs regularisation”, “N unpaired”, “N outside window”, or a green “clean” badge. Status is never hand-picked: it comes from the rules published in config/attendance-rules.json, evaluated by the platform rule engine. An expandable “How was <day> classified?” panel under the table prints the full decision trace for the most recent settled day. Below that, “What this month earned” lists any day that earned a comp-off or recorded overtime, with a “Credit this month's comp-offs” button (safe to press more than once — each posting names its own source day, so nothing is credited twice; overtime is recorded, never priced, since no multiplier is declared anywhere in this build). A final “Regularisation” card lists this employee's own correction requests (day, missing punch, reason, state) with inline Approve/Reject for whoever can decide, and its own “raise a request” form at the bottom.

An expandable “Why this report cannot disagree with the payslip” note explains that every cell is the same settlement engine and the same config/attendance-rules.json the payslip pays from — no second pairing pass, no second shift window, no invented punches for a day with none. A Period bar (Month / Year / MTD / Custom, up to the configured months-at-a-time ceiling) plus a Who row of company/branch/department/designation/team dropdowns (From/To dates and a Show button) narrow what's read; an “Export CSV” button downloads whichever view is currently open. att-manual.g: One punch now, or a whole register sheet — the sheet always waits for approval
att-manual.w: Reached as “Manual Entry” from the menu. If you hold manual-punch rights, a “Single punch” card lets you pick an Employee (by id, never free-typed — two people can share a name, so an id-based dropdown is the only way this can never punch the wrong person), Date, Time and Direction (In/Out), and “Add” applies it immediately, the same as a real device punch. Below it, if you hold bulk-upload rights, a “Bulk upload” card takes a CSV in one of two templates — “one row per employee-day” (code, name, date, in, out) or “one row per punch” (code, name, date, time, in/out; use this one for a night shift, one row per punch on its own date) — both downloadable from buttons right there. Uploading writes nothing to attendance by itself: every row is checked (who it names, whether the date and times actually parse, whether out is after in) and kept with its own verdict — Pending, Refused (with the reason printed), or, once decided, Approved/Rejected. A “Batches” table (Loaded, By, Rows, Pending, Refused, Approved, Rejected, Decided, and an “Open” link) lists every sheet ever loaded; opening one shows its row-by-row table (Line, Employee, As written, Date, In, Out, State, Reason) with an “Approve N pending row(s) → punches” / “Reject the batch” pair for whoever holds approval rights, and a per-row “Withdraw” for a row that shouldn't be decided as-is (a withdrawn row stays listed, not deleted, so the file and the batch always agree line for line). Approving turns each approved row into an ordinary punch carrying source=bulk and the batch/line it came from, so approving the same batch twice never doubles anyone's attendance.

biometric-devices.g: Loading device export files, plus the device and pending-punch registers behind them
biometric-devices.w: This one help key covers three screens reached from the Time & Attendance menu. “ZKTeco Devices” (route punch-import, titled “Import punches” on screen) is the working import tool: a “Load an export” form takes the device's own export file plus a named Layout (from config/punch-layouts.json — the layout is always named, never auto-detected, because reading one device model's file with another's column order parses cleanly and means something else entirely) and an optional “Dry run” checkbox that reports what would happen — how many punches parsed, which device user ids map to nobody — without writing a single row. A device user id that matches no employee is reported and refused, never silently dropped or guessed at; re-importing the same file is always safe, since a punch is identified by its device, person, instant and direction, not by which file it arrived in. “Biometric Devices” (menu item “Biometric Devices”, a generic module register) is the device catalogue: Name, Serial/Device ID, Company, Branch, Location, Punch Direction (Auto/In/Out), the device's API URL and Comm Key for LAN/WebAPI-mode devices, Status (Active/Offline/Error/Retired) and Last sync — an ordinary Add/Edit/Delete table. “Pending Punches” is a second generic register of punches a device sent that could not yet be matched to an employee: Punched at, Device, Device user ID, Direction, Verified by (Fingerprint/Face/Card/Password/Other) — resolving one usually means enrolling that device user id against the right employee and re-importing, rather than editing the pending row itself.

Dry run reports parse results and unmapped device user ids without writing anything
Biometric Devices register: Add a device with its serial, connection mode and credentials

biometric-devices.tip: Re-importing the exact same export file is always safe — a punch is identified by device, person, instant and direction, so nothing is ever duplicated by loading a file twice.
biometric-devices.rel: Also see: Manual & Bulk Attendance, Attendance, Attendance Report
biometric-devices.why: Every biometric device in this market exports a delimited log — that file is the universal interface, not a vendor SDK. What differs between models is only the column order, so layouts live as data in config/punch-layouts.json: a new device model is a config edit, not a release, and naming the layout on every import (instead of guessing it) is what stops one device's file being silently misread as another's.

Dry run lets a brand-new device's file be checked before anything is written
Importing the same file twice can never double anyone's attendance

leave-apply.g: One employee's balance, policy and requests — the balance is never a stored number
leave-apply.w: This screen has no menu entry of its own yet — it's reached by an employee's own “Leave” link (from the Employee Directory, Notifications, or the Holiday/Weekly-Off screen) with that person's id. With no employee chosen it just says so and links back to Employees; there is no employee picker on this screen itself. Once opened, three stat cards show Days (the EL balance as at today), Days after all approved leave (as at the furthest-out approved request's end date — shown separately because an approved request starting next week does not move today's balance), and Requests on record. An expandable “Why the balance is not a stored column” note explains that every figure is SUM(credits) − SUM(debits) over the ledger as at the date asked about, computed live — never read from a saved number. “The leave policy” table (from config/leave-policy.json, narrowed to the types this employee's marital status qualifies for) lists, per type: its code and name, whether it's Paid, days on joining, monthly accrual, the cap, and this person's balance today — the same paid/unpaid list payroll itself reads, so leave and payroll can never disagree about whether a day was paid. Accrual is posted to the ledger monthly, one named entry per month, so refreshing this page never grows the balance by itself. If you may submit a request, a “Request leave” form takes From, To and a Reason and submits it as EL — the type is fixed, not a dropdown; weekends are excluded from the day count, and holidays/weekly-off rosters are not yet wired into that count (named directly in the screen's own note as the next piece of work still to come). The “Requests” table lists every request (Dates, Days, Reason, a State badge, who decided it and their note); a pending row, for whoever can decide, gets an inline form where From/To can be edited before approving — approving a different range than what was asked recomputes the days rather than taking a typed number — plus a required Remarks box and Approve/Reject buttons. A rejected request never touches the ledger. At the bottom, “The ledger” prints the raw statement of every credit and debit behind the balance above — a cancelled approval would show as a reversal entry, never a deletion, so the evidence that leave was approved and then withdrawn is never lost.

The leave policy table — paid/unpaid, accrual and cap per type, from config, not code
Request leave: From, To and a Reason — always filed as EL, there is no type picker yet
Approve (optionally adjusting the dates) or Reject a pending request, with a required remark
The ledger — the literal statement of every credit and debit behind the balance shown above

Check the two balance figures and the policy table before deciding anything.
To apply: fill in From, To and a Reason under “Request leave”, and submit — it always files as EL today.
To decide a pending request: adjust From/To if the approved range should differ from what was asked, add a required remark, and Approve or Reject.
Read “The ledger” at the bottom if a balance figure needs explaining down to the individual posting.
leave-apply.tip: Approving with edited From/To dates approves that edited range, not the originally requested one — the day count is recomputed from what you approved, never typed in by hand.
leave-apply.rel: Also see: Employees, Approvals Inbox, Holiday / Weekly-Off Schedule
leave-apply.why: A balance kept as a stored column can only ever answer one question at a time, and it drifts the moment anyone touches it directly. Computing it from ledger postings, on read, at whichever date is asked about, means “what do I have today” and “what will I have once this approved leave lands” are both always correct — and both readable straight from the same entries, never from two different code paths.

leave-types.g: Every part of the Leave types screen, explained
