holidays.w: A Year picker (type any year or choose from the list — the schedule outlives whatever years it shipped with) plus links to Leave & Absence and Shifts. The “W.OFF schedule” card sets the weekly-off pattern: a quick-pattern dropdown (e.g. “Every Sunday”) or manual day/nth-occurrence ticks, saved per company (or the shipped default until you save your own). Below it, the year's holiday list: each holiday can be marked Recurring (shows on every year automatically — a fixed holiday like New Year's Day is not re-entered annually) or dated to one specific year, and each carries its own scope — Company, Branch, Role, Designation checkboxes, defaulting to Any/everyone until narrowed. Attendance rules, the muster roll, leave calculations and payroll proration all read this one schedule directly — there is no second copy of “what day is a holiday” anywhere else in the product.

Marking a holiday Recurring makes it show up on every year's schedule automatically, with no need to re-add it
Each holiday's own scope checkboxes (Company/Branch/Role/Designation) narrow who it applies to — blank means everyone
Saving the W.OFF schedule for the first time turns the shipped default into this company's own, customised pattern

Set the weekly-off pattern once via a quick preset, or tick the exact days/occurrences manually.

holidays.rel: Leave & Absence and Shifts (header buttons) both read this same schedule.
holidays.why: One shared schedule that attendance, leave and payroll all read directly — rather than each keeping its own holiday list — is what stops a holiday changed in one place and forgotten in another from silently disagreeing about which day was worked.
holidays.uc: A regional holiday applies only to the Hyderabad branch, not company-wide. It's added once, scoped to that branch, marked recurring if it falls on the same date every year — and from that point on, attendance, leave and payroll for Hyderabad employees automatically treat that date as a holiday, while every other branch's proration is untouched.

salary-setup.g: Two screens under one guide: Salary Components, then Salary Structure
salary-setup.w: This help entry covers two screens reached from the same Payroll Setup area. “Salary Components” is the plain catalogue table — columns Code, Name, Type (Earning/Deduction badge), Calc type, Value (% or amount), Taxable?, Seq (the order it prints on the payslip), Company (blank = ALL), Base; “Add Salary component” opens a form with those same fields plus Applies To (Company/Team/Employee) and, for earnings, Category (Fixed/Variable/Reimbursement) — this is simply naming what components exist (HRA, PF, conveyance…), not who gets how much of them. “Salary Structure” is the screen that actually assigns rates: a header shows three legend badges (earning / deduction / employer cost) and, for anyone without payroll.structure.publish, a read-only table of every component rule in force today — Component, Calculation, Applies to (the scope it was published for, or “everybody”), Rate, Detail (its formula in plain text). For a publisher, the same information becomes an editable grid: an “Effective from” date and a “Why” note at the top (required context for every publish), then one compact summary line per rule that expands into a full field grid on its own Edit button, an “Add component” button, and a sticky “Save all rules” button at the grid's bottom edge that publishes the entire set together. Each rule picks exactly one calculation shape — a flat % of a basis, a flat amount, a manual formula (parentheses and system values: calendar days, working days, # Hours capped by Overtime Pay's Max OT hours), a slab table, or a status-based rule (checked against real employee columns like PCC Status, DRA Status, PAN or National ID) — picking one locks the other controls on that row.
f: Salary Components → “Add Salary component” defines a new pay item (its code, name, type, taxability, print order)
Salary Structure → “Add component” adds a new rule row to the grid — who gets that component and at what rate
Each grid row's own Edit/Done toggle expands or collapses it — the list stays scannable without a sideways-scrolling table
“Save all rules” validates and publishes the whole grid together — never one row at a time, and never partially
“Effective from” + “Why” are required on every publish — the prior rules close the day before, so a March payslip still recomputes from March's rule
s: First, make sure the component itself exists in Salary Components (code, name, Earning/Deduction, taxability).
Then in Salary Structure, click “Add component,” pick that component and a scope (company, branch, team, designation or employee — leave scope fields blank for everybody).
Pick exactly one calculation shape for the row: percentage, flat amount, formula, slab, or status rule.
Set “Effective from” and a “Why” note, then “Save all rules” — the whole grid is checked before anything is written; one bad row refuses the entire publish.
To confirm what's live without editing, anyone without publish rights sees the same information as a plain read-only table.
salary-setup.tip: If a warning banner says rules are being kept in a file rather than in MySQL, nothing is broken — it is the product's own database-not-migrated-yet fallback, effective-dated exactly the same way. It names the two commands that move it into MySQL; that is Shashank's / the dev team's step, not something to run from this screen.
salary-setup.rel: Salary Components and Salary Structure are two separate screens under Payroll Setup; Salary Structure's own component dropdown is filled from whatever Salary Components currently declares.
salary-setup.why: Splitting “what components exist” from “who gets which, at what rate” means a company-wide component (say PF) is declared once and then scoped as many times as needed — head office at one rate, a field branch at another — without redeclaring the component itself each time. Publishing the whole grid as one all-or-nothing set (never row by row) is what stops a half-saved structure from ever being the thing payroll actually runs against.
salary-setup.uc: Mumbai's conveyance allowance needs to rise from ₹2,000 to ₹2,400 starting next month. The Conveyance component already exists in Salary Components, so this is purely a Salary Structure change: open the existing Mumbai-scoped row, change its flat amount to 2400, set Effective from to the 1st, note “Mumbai conveyance raised to 2,400”, and Save all rules — the old rate closes the day before, the new one opens exactly on the 1st, and a payslip re-run for last month still uses ₹2,000.
adv: One shared catalogue (Salary Components) feeds every scoped rule in Salary Structure — a component is never redefined per scope
The whole rule set validates and publishes together, so a payroll run never sees a half-updated structure
Every publish is effective-dated, so re-printing an old payslip always recomputes against the rule that was actually in force then
mk: Adding a new component directly as a Salary Structure rule without first declaring it in Salary Components
The rule references a component code the catalogue doesn't recognise, and publishing the set is refused outright
Add the component in Salary Components first (code, name, type), then scope and rate it in Salary Structure
Setting more than one calculation shape on the same rule row (e.g. both a percentage and a formula)
The controls lock each other out on purpose — only the shape you pick last stays editable, the rest grey out
Pick the one calculation shape the rule actually needs before filling in its value

How often this schedule pays; “Lots”. How many disbursement lots in a cycle (1 = one payout; 2 = two lots, e.g. 7th and 22nd); “Applicable To” — a dropdown. salary-gen.g: One screen, three doors: Generate, Approve, and the register itself
salary-gen.w: This one screen (internally called the register) is reached three ways, and shows a different top section depending on which menu item brought you here, but the same list of closed periods below it every time. “Generate Payroll” shows a “Close a period” card: an organisation filter (Company/Branch/Department/Designation/Role/Team/Employee, live from Organization Configuration — it only narrows the on-screen preview count, the close itself always covers every employee), a “Pick by” selector (Month, or a custom From/To date range), and “Compute and close.” “Salary Approval” shows the same list of runs but each one now leads with its approval controls instead of the close form: a row of numbered stage badges (green = done, amber = next, grey = not yet), a text box plus button for the next approval step, and, once at least one step is done, “Reject” and “Request re-submission” boxes (each requires a reason). The plain “Payroll register” view (reached from the sidebar item of that name) shows every run with no close form and no approval controls, purely for reference. In all three, every closed period is a card: four stat tiles (Employees, Gross earnings, Deductions, Net for the month), a “reproduced” / “not reproduced” badge (does recomputing this run today give the same figures on file), an “approved” / “not approved” badge, a “Bank advice” table (account, IFSC, arrears portion, amount, a running total, and the same data as a CSV block beneath it), a “Raise a correction” box (recomputes today's figures and stores only the difference — the original run is never edited), and, once approved, a “Reverse this month” control.
f: The organisation filter on Generate Payroll narrows the preview count only — the close itself is always the whole company
“Compute and close” turns a month (or a custom date range, closed to its calendar month) into a run — closed runs are never silently recomputed
On Salary Approval, the button beside the reason box advances the run to its next configured approval stage
“Reject” and “Request re-submission” both withdraw a run — neither edits it; both require a typed reason
“Reverse this month” (approved runs only) records the opposite of an approved run as a second entry, carried into the next close as arrears
“Raise a correction” recomputes today's figures and stores only the difference beside the untouched original
Pay Cycle & Lots / Payslips / Ledger buttons in the header jump to the three screens that read this run's output
s: To close a new period: open Generate Payroll, optionally filter to preview a subset, pick Month or a custom range, and click “Compute and close.”
To approve a closed run: open Salary Approval, type a note in the box for the next stage, and click its button — repeat for each configured stage until the run shows “Approved for payment.”
A negative-net payslip in the run blocks approval outright until it is looked at — the run lists exactly which employee codes and amounts, right in the card.

If a closed run turns out wrong before approval, Reject or Request re-submission with a reason; after approval, use Reverse this month instead — either way a new record is made, nothing is edited in place.
To fix a live discrepancy in an already-closed run without reversing it, use “Raise a correction” — it stores the delta, not a replacement.
Use the Bank advice table/CSV on an approved run to actually pay it; an employee with missing bank details is named and blocks the file rather than being silently skipped.
salary-gen.tip: The person who closed a run can never also approve it — the button for the next stage simply will not show for them, even if they hold the approval permission. That is enforced here, not just documented.
salary-gen.rel: Header buttons on this screen: Pay Cycle & Lots, Payslips, Ledger. Reached from the sidebar as Generate Payroll, Salary Approval, or Payroll register — all three are this one screen.
salary-gen.why: A payroll run is one whole-month control total, not a bundle of individual payslips — so it is closed once, as a whole, and never quietly recomputed: two people asking “what did we pay in March” must always get the same answer from the same system. Corrections and reversals both add a new record instead of editing the old one, for the same reason invoices are credit-noted rather than rewritten.
salary-gen.uc: A run is closed for September, then a missing punch is found for one employee on the 3rd. Nobody edits September: “Raise a correction” recomputes today's figures, stores just that employee's delta next to the untouched original run, and the difference is carried forward and paid as an arrears line the next time a period is closed — so “what did September actually pay” and “what do we now owe” both stay answerable.
adv: One shared screen for close, approve and review — the approval workflow can never drift out of sync with what was actually closed
The closer-cannot-approve rule and the negative-net block are enforced in the same place the button would otherwise appear
Every after-the-fact change (correction, reversal) is its own new record, so “what was paid” never stops matching history
mk: Trying to fix a wrong closed run by editing employee records and waiting for the next close
The wrong month stays wrong on file forever — a later close only affects the next period, not the one already closed
Use “Raise a correction” on the closed run itself; it recomputes and records exactly the difference against that period
Approving a run that shows a negative-net payslip warning
Approval is refused outright for that run until the flagged employee(s) are resolved — there is no override
Reject or request re-submission, fix the underlying figure, then let the next close (or a correction) produce a clean run

salary-approval.w: Generated runs wait here for a second pair of eyes. The approver sees totals and per-employee lines, can send back with remarks, or approve — after which payslips are published and emailed.
s: Open the pending run and scan the totals against last month.
Drill into any odd line.
Approve — payslips go live and employees are emailed.
salary-approval.tip: Compare the net-total with the previous month first — a big jump is the fastest error detector.
salary-approval.why: Money should never move on one person's click. The approval step is your four-eyes control — the same discipline banks demand of you, applied to your own payroll.
salary-approval.uc: Picture this: the approver compares this month's total to last month's, spots a ₹2 lakh jump, drills in, finds a wrongly-entered bonus — caught BEFORE the bank file went out, not after.
adv: Errors caught before money leaves
Owner control without owner workload
Clean separation of preparer and approver
mk: Approving without comparing to last month's total
The fastest error-detector is skipped — big mistakes ride through
First look: net total vs last month; investigate any swing before line-level review

payslip.g: Three screens under one guide: the Payslips grid, one Payslip, and the Format Designer
payslip.w: “Payslips” opens on the most recently closed run and shows a “Month / closed run” dropdown plus the usual Company/Branch/Department/Designation/Role/Team filters, then four stat tiles (Payslips, Total gross, Total deductions, Total net pay) and a searchable table: Code, Employee (with company beneath the name), Gross, Deductions, Net, Status (approved/draft badge), and a small PDF icon that opens that one person's payslip. “Print all as PDF” switches the same page into a print layout — every visible payslip laid out one after another, using your browser's own Print-to-PDF rather than a bundled PDF library, so the printed copy is generated by the exact same code as the on-screen and single-payslip views and can never drift from them. “Export CSV” downloads the grid as shown. Any employee in the closed run who could not produce a payslip is named above the grid, not silently dropped from the count. Opening one payslip (the PDF icon, or Payslip Format Designer's own preview) shows a single printable page: company logo and colour pulled from that employee's own employer record (never the app's own branding), the period picker if more than one closed run exists for that employee, and the earnings/deductions laid out in whichever Payslip Format currently applies to that employee's company/branch/department/designation — resolved by the same most-specific-wins scope ladder Salary Structure uses. The “Payslip Format Designer” (a separate screen) is where that layout is built: a context bar to pick which company/branch/team/designation/role a format applies to, a rail listing every saved format, a drag-and-drop editor built from the real Salary Components catalogue (never invented placeholder components), and a live payslip preview on the right that always reflects your own company's actual logo, colour and address — saved to the server per tenant, not to the browser, so a format one person designs is the format everyone in that scope actually gets.
f: Month / closed run dropdown plus the standard org filters narrow the Payslips grid to one period and one slice of the company
“Print all as PDF” renders every visible payslip as one print job via the browser's own Print-to-PDF
“Export CSV” downloads exactly the rows currently shown in the grid
The small icon at the end of each grid row opens that one employee's single payslip
Payslip Format Designer's rail switches between every saved format; its context bar decides which company/branch/team/designation/role a format you're editing applies to
s: Pick a closed run from the Month / closed run dropdown — nothing prints until a run is chosen.
Narrow with the org filters if you only need one branch, department or role's payslips.
Use the search box to jump to one person by name or code within the chosen run.
Click the PDF icon on a row for one person's payslip, or “Print all as PDF” for everyone currently shown.

To change how a payslip looks (not what it contains), go to Payslip Format Designer, pick the scope you want to change, edit the layout, and save — it takes effect for everyone in that scope immediately.
payslip.tip: The batch grid, the single payslip, and the print-all view all read the same closed run through the same code — there is no separate print renderer to fall out of sync, so what an employee's own payslip shows is always exactly what the grid and the printed copy say too.
payslip.rel: Payslips (grid) → one Payslip (PDF icon) → Payslip Format Designer (layout, separate screen, needs payroll.structure access).
payslip.why: A second, separate print layout is the layout that quietly drifts from the screen version over time — someone adds a component on-screen and forgets the PDF template. Reading print, grid and single-payslip off the same underlying code removes that failure mode entirely, at the cost of relying on the browser's own PDF export instead of a nicer bundled one.
payslip.uc: Payroll for September closes, and Finance needs a CSV of net pay by branch for a bank reconciliation. Open Payslips, pick 2026-09 from Month / closed run, filter Branch to the one needed, and Export CSV — the totals in that file match the four stat tiles above it and the individual payslips employees see, because all three come from the same closed run.
adv: One code path for screen, PDF and print — a payslip can never show one figure on screen and a different one printed
Refused payslips are named on the grid, not silently missing from the count
Format changes are scoped and saved server-side, so everyone in that scope sees the same layout at once
mk: Assuming a payslip that fails to generate is simply skipped from the batch
It's named explicitly above the grid with its own reason — missing it there means missing why one employee has no payslip this month
Always check the refused-employee notice above the grid before treating a batch as complete

pay-ledger.g: Every part of this read-only ledger, explained
pay-ledger.w: This screen merges four sources into one dated list, each row naming exactly where it came from: payslips (from a closed payroll run), commissions and commission payments (from Compensation & Claims), and deductions (from the Deductions Ledger). At the top, an employee dropdown (“All employees” or one specific person) and, when no period filter is active, a month picker. Below that, a Period bar (the usual month / year / financial year / YTD / MTD / custom-range picker, with a “Show every period” link to clear it) and a Who bar (the standard Company/Branch/Department/Designation/Role/Team filters). Four KPI tiles follow: earned (salary lines plus commissions), paid out / deducted (payments plus deductions), balance (earned minus paid), and entries (how many rows are in the current view). The table itself: Date / month, Employee, Kind (a green badge for salary/commission, amber for payment/deduction), Entry (a plain-language label, e.g. “Payslip 2026-09” or “Deduction late …”), Credit (green, what was earned), Debit (red, what was paid out or deducted), Status, and Source (the exact record reference, e.g. payslip:412, that row was built from).
f: Employee dropdown switches between one person and every employee this account may read
The Period bar and the Who bar both filter every row on the page — they combine, they don't replace each other
“Show every period” clears only the period filter, keeping whichever employee and org filters are set
Every row's Source column is a direct reference to the record it was built from — nothing here is a stored figure of its own
s: Pick one employee, or leave “All employees” to see everyone this account may read.
Narrow by Period (a month, a year, a financial year, YTD/MTD, or a custom range) and by the Who filters (Company, Branch, Department, Designation, Role, Team) as needed.
Read the four KPI tiles for a quick earned/paid/balance/entry-count summary of exactly what's filtered in below.
Use the Source column on any row to find and open the actual payslip, commission, payment or deduction record it came from — this screen has no edit or delete of its own.
pay-ledger.tip: This ledger is deliberately read-only: nothing here can be changed on this page. To correct a figure, open the actual source screen named in the Source column — Generate Payroll for a salary line, Compensation & Claims for a commission, or the Deductions Ledger for a deduction.
pay-ledger.rel: Its four sources live on their own screens: Generate Payroll (salary lines), Compensation & Claims (commissions and payments), Deductions Ledger.
pay-ledger.why: A payroll team is regularly asked “what did this person earn and get paid across these three months, from every source,” and answering that from four separate screens is how a manual reconciliation quietly leaves one commission or one deduction out. Merging them here, read-only, means the answer is always built from the same four sources rather than a fifth number someone typed once and never updates.
pay-ledger.uc: An employee disputes a deduction on their September pay. Pick their name, set Period to September, and every line touching them that month is on one page — the payslip credit, any commission, and the deduction itself with its own Source reference — so it's immediately clear whether the deduction was applied once or, by mistake, twice.
adv: One page answers “what happened to this person's pay this period,” across all four sources
Every row can be traced back to its exact source record, never a number typed here directly
Read-only end to end, so the ledger itself can never become the thing that's wrong

pay-cycle.w: This page has three parts. mobile-devices.w: When an employee installs the SmartPRS app and enters your company web address, their phone appears here as Pending. mobile-devices.tip: The device gate is your anti-fraud lock — approve deliberately, and revoke the moment a phone goes missing. No background tracking is used; punch GPS is foreground-only.
mobile-devices.why: A phone that can punch attendance from anywhere is also a phone that could fake it from anywhere, so approval is a deliberate human decision rather than automatic on first install — the same reason a punch's GPS is foreground-only. mobile-devices.uc: Picture this: a field agent's phone is lost on the commute home. You open Mobile Devices, find their entry and tap Revoke — on its next check the phone loses access, before whoever has it can punch attendance or see anyone's data.

advance.g: A cash advance against salary, recovered automatically as payroll closes
advance.w: Reached only at its direct module URL today — “Advances” has no sidebar entry yet. It is an ordinary Add/Edit/Delete register: Employee (looked up by code and name), Amount, a Status badge (Requested, Approved, Disbursed, Recovering, Recovered, Written off) and Remarks. Once an advance is Disbursed, it is not left for someone to remember and deduct by hand: every payroll run that closes from here on recovers an instalment against it automatically, exactly like an ordinary deduction line on the payslip. The Amount column shown on this register is the original, opening figure — nothing on this screen writes to it directly; what has actually been recovered so far is worked out from the closed payroll runs themselves, so reversing a closed month reverses that month's recovery along with it, rather than leaving the register's own numbers to be corrected by hand.

Status moves to Recovering while instalments are still being taken, and to Recovered once the balance reaches zero.

A tenant that needs overtime paid out today does so outside this figure, until a pricing rule and a payslip line are built on top of it.

s: Generate the letter for the candidate — details flow in from Recruitment.
Send it; the candidate opens the link and accepts.
HR confirms the hire from the pipeline once accepted.
letters-offer.tip: Edit the standard template once with your tone and terms — every letter after that is consistent.
letters-offer.why: Candidates judge a company by its offer letter — and chase-up calls kill momentum. Branded letters with one-tap acceptance close candidates while they're still excited.
letters-offer.uc: Picture this: walk-in Thursday, offer Friday morning, accepted from his phone by Friday lunch, joined Monday — before a competitor's call could reach him.
adv: Faster acceptance, fewer dropouts
Professional first impression
Acceptance status without phone chasing
mk: Editing CTC by hand in a generated letter
The letter and the system disagree — a dispute waiting for its day
Fix the figure on the candidate/offer record and regenerate; never hand-edit

s: Approve the increment under Compensation — the letter sends itself.
Re-issue happens automatically if the approved figures are corrected.
letters-increment.tip: You rarely open this screen — the increment flow does the work; this is the archive.
letters-increment.why: The raise letter is the trophy employees show their families. Automatic, accurate, branded — it turns payroll arithmetic into a motivation event.
letters-increment.uc: Picture this: approval at 11 AM, letter in her inbox at 11:01. The moment of pride arrives at full speed.
adv: Zero gap between decision and delight
Figures always match the approved record
Archive ready for any reference

letters-warning.w: Issue formal warnings — misconduct, absenteeism, policy breach — from templates, keeping a dated record on the employee's file.
s: Generate the letter citing the specific incident and date.
Issue it and keep the acknowledgement.
letters-warning.tip: Specific beats general — "absent 4, 5, 6 June without intimation" stands in any review; "frequent absence" does not.
letters-warning.why: Discipline without documentation becomes he-said-she-said in any tribunal. Warning letters create the progressive record that protects fair employers.
letters-warning.uc: Picture this: a termination is challenged. You produce three dated warnings with specific incidents — the matter ends in the meeting room, not the court room.
adv: Progressive discipline, provable
Specific incidents beat vague accusations
Fairness visible to everyone watching
mk: Writing vague warnings ("poor behaviour")
Vague warnings collapse under questioning — the record protects nobody
Cite specific incidents with dates; specificity is the entire protection

letters-relieving.w: Relieving and experience letters for departing staff — dates and designation auto-filled from the record, issued after the Full & Final settles.
s: Complete the exit and F&F first.
Generate and issue the letter.
letters-relieving.tip: Issue promptly after settlement — delayed relieving letters generate the angriest follow-ups.
letters-relieving.why: A leaver's last document shapes their last impression — and their review of you. Prompt relieving letters close chapters cleanly.
letters-relieving.uc: Picture this: F&F settled Monday, letter issued Monday. The next employer verifies; everything matches; your reputation compounds.
adv: Clean endings protect reputation
Details auto-filled — no manual errors
Alumni goodwill, cheaply earned

letters-templates.w: The master templates behind every letter — edit the wording, add placeholders like candidate name, CTC and joining date, and every future letter follows.
s: Open the template for the letter type.
Adjust wording; keep the placeholders intact.
Generate one test letter to verify.
letters-templates.tip: Placeholders are typed in double curly braces — remove one and that detail silently disappears from letters, so test after editing.
letters-templates.why: Letters written fresh each time drift — wording, clauses, tone. Templates lock your best version as the only version.
letters-templates.uc: Picture this: legal suggests one clause change. You edit the template once; every letter from tomorrow carries it.
adv: Consistency without vigilance
Legal changes applied once, everywhere
Placeholders kill copy-paste errors
mk: Deleting a placeholder while editing wording
That detail silently disappears from every future letter
Keep the double-curly placeholders intact; generate one test letter after every edit

send-message.w: Compose and send a message to chosen employees, teams or everyone — delivered by email, for announcements that need to land personally rather than on the notice board.
s: Pick the audience.
Write a clear subject and short body; send.
send-message.tip: For standing information use the Notice Board; use direct messages for things that need action.
send-message.why: Important instructions sent on WhatsApp groups drown in good-morning messages. Direct, recorded messages make critical communication land and stay provable.
send-message.uc: Picture this: a bank changes the deposit process effective tomorrow. You message all field staff tonight — recorded, dated. Tomorrow, "I didn't know" is not available.
adv: Critical instructions provably delivered
Targeted — only who needs it
A record where group chats have none
mk: Broadcasting everything to everyone
Real instructions drown; people stop reading
Target the audience that must act; use the Notice Board for general info

notice-board.w: Publish notices — holidays, policy updates, winners — visible to everyone on their dashboard. The digital equivalent of the board at reception, minus the pins.
s: Add the notice with a clear title and date.
It appears on dashboards immediately.
notice-board.tip: Old notices clutter fast — retire them monthly so the board stays believable.
notice-board.why: A company's notice board is its public voice to employees. A live one — on every dashboard — keeps the whole group hearing the same thing at the same time.
notice-board.uc: Picture this: revised office timing from Monday. One notice, every dashboard, all companies — and the WhatsApp rumour version never forms.
adv: One announcement, full reach
Rumours pre-empted by official word
Dated history of every announcement
mk: Leaving expired notices up for months
The board loses credibility; new notices get ignored
Retire old notices monthly — a fresh board is a read board

kpi-achievements.w: The one live item in the Performance & Rewards menu. A “Whose KPIs” card holds an Employee ID lookup (with an autocomplete list of active employees) and a Show-this-profile button; with nothing typed it defaults to your own linked employee record, and a “My own profile” link returns to that after looking someone else up. Once a profile resolves, a summary strip shows their initials, name and code plus a badge counting how many KPIs are kept for their company/branch/role today — a KPI only ever appears here once it is ticked Keep for that scope under Organization Setup / Configuration → KRAs and KPIs. If you hold employee.update and at least one KPI is kept for the profile, a “Record an achievement” form appears: a KPI dropdown grouped by KRA (showing, for an achievement-role KPI, which target KPI it measures against), a Period type (Month, or a custom date range — the month field and the from/to fields show and hide together depending which is picked), and an Achieved value field, with a Record button. The achieved figure is measured against whatever target is configured for that KPI and scope — a kept KPI with no target agreed yet is refused rather than guessed at, and the resulting % Achieved is computed exactly and only rounded for display. A “Recorded” table underneath lists every achievement ever logged (Employee, KPI, Period, Target, Achieved, a colour-coded % Achieved badge — green at 100%+, amber at 75%+, red below — and who recorded it, when).

kpi-achievements.uc: A manager opens an executive's profile, sees “Collection Amount” kept for their branch, records this month's achieved figure against the agreed target, and the row immediately shows a green 100%+ badge confirming the target was met.
adv: An achievement can never be logged against a KPI the scoring engine wouldn't recognise

Search filters the table by Title. Each row's Edit re-opens the same form pre-filled; Delete retires a row rather than erasing it — a superseded policy is meant to be marked Superseded and kept, not deleted, so the history of what the policy used to say is never lost. This is a newly-added module — until now, opening “Policy Repository” from the menu had nothing configured behind it.

policies.why: A policy with no version, owner or review date is a document nobody can be held to — this register makes each policy's currency (is it still the active one?) and its next review date explicit, rather than leaving that knowledge in one person's head.
policies.uc: HR uploads a revised Leave Policy as v2.0, marks the old v1.0 row Superseded rather than deleting it, and sets a review-due date a year out so it doesn't go stale unnoticed.
adv: A policy's version history is kept, not overwritten — Superseded rows stay on record
A review-due date makes a stale policy visible instead of silently forgotten

statutory-bonus.g: Payment of Bonus Act working per employee for a financial year — eligible months, wage counted, bonus at both ends of the band
statutory-bonus.w: For a chosen financial year, which months qualify for each employee (the bonus wage that month must be at most the eligibility ceiling in config/statutory-bonus.json), what wage is counted (capped at the calculation ceiling) and what the bonus comes to at both the minimum and maximum percent of that band. The bonus wage for a month is read from the closed run's lines flagged as bonus wage under the salary structure in force then — never projected. Three totals sit above the table (closed runs in the year, and the total at each percentage), and every row can expand to show the month-by-month working: which months were eligible, what wage each counted, and why a month over the ceiling did not count. Actual bonus paid is recorded separately on the Bonus Register — this screen computes the exposure, it does not itself pay anything.
f: Pick a financial year; totals and rows recompute from that year's closed runs
Bonus at both the minimum and maximum percent of the band, side by side
Per-employee month-by-month working, expandable, showing why a month did or didn't count
"Bonus register" link — what was actually declared and paid, as its own register
s: Pick the financial year and press Show to see that year's eligible months and bonus exposure.
Expand a row's "months" detail to see exactly which months counted and at what wage.
Record what is actually declared and paid on the Bonus Register — this screen is the computed exposure, not the payment record.
statutory-bonus.tip: Working days below the Act's minimum are not judged on this screen — attendance is the Time section's word, not payroll's — so a low-attendance employee still shows their computed exposure here even if the Act would exclude them on working days alone.
statutory-bonus.rel: Also see: Bonus Register, Bonus & Encashment, Statutory Configuration
statutory-bonus.why: A bonus figure projected from CTC before the year's runs have even closed is a promise, not a liability. Reading the bonus wage from closed runs only, month by month, means the number on this screen is always something that already happened in payroll, not something payroll might do.
statutory-bonus.uc: Picture this: finance wants the FY24-25 statutory bonus exposure before the Bonus Register is filled in. You pick that financial year, read the totals at min and max percent, and have a defensible range without waiting for every payment to be recorded.
adv: Bonus wage always comes from closed runs and the structure version in force then — never a mid-year guess
A month over the eligibility ceiling is marked as not counting, with the reason visible in its own working
Min and max percent are shown together, so the real exposure range is visible at a glance

audit-reports.g: Every statutory register an inspector could ask for, with a row count and a CSV export, in one place
audit-reports.w: The registers declared in config/audit-reports.json — each with its source (a table, or a figure computed on another screen), a row count scoped by the Organization Setup filter below, and its columns — plus a one-click CSV export for each. A register with no employee column is exported whole, since the org filter has nothing to scope it by. A confidential register (POSH complaints, for instance) never gets a bulk export button — only an "Open" link into its own screen, where its own access rules decide what is shown. Every export this screen produces is itself written to the audit trail, naming the register and the row count, and money columns export as the exact decimal strings stored, never as floats.
f: Every declared register, with its source, row count and columns
One-click CSV export per register, scoped by the Organization Setup filter
A confidential register gets "Open" only — never a bulk export button
Every export is itself logged to the audit trail with the register and row count
s: Open Audit Reports before an inspection to see every register in one place, with current row counts.
Use the Organization Setup filter to scope an export to one company, branch or team.
For a confidential register, use "Open" — there is no bulk export, by design.
audit-reports.tip: "Rows in view" changes with the Organization Setup filter — an unscoped export and a filtered one can show different counts for the same register, which is expected, not a discrepancy to chase.
r: Whoever the register's own permission in config/audit-reports.json grants — not one fixed role for the whole screen
audit-reports.rel: Also see: Statutory Configuration, Activity Logs, POSH Complaints
audit-reports.why: An inspector asking for a register mid-audit is not the moment to discover which table it lives in or write a one-off export script. Declaring every register once, with its own confidentiality flag, means the answer to "can I see X" is already decided before anyone asks.
audit-reports.uc: Picture this: a statutory audit asks for the PF register for one branch. You open Audit Reports, filter to that branch, and download the CSV — the export itself is now on the audit trail too, so there's a record that it was produced and when.
adv: Every register an inspector might ask for lives in one declared list, not scattered across screens someone has to remember
A confidential register cannot be bulk-exported by construction — the button for it does not exist
Exports are themselves audited, so "who pulled this register, and when" is never a separate question

pf-esi-register.g: Per-employee PF/ESI registration record — a plain generic register
pf-esi-register.w: A generic-module list of each employee's PF/ESI registration status: Employee, UAN, ESI IP number, whether PF and ESI registration is done (checkboxes) and the date registered. Add, edit and delete rows the same way as any other generic module screen — orange button to add, pencil to edit, trash to delete.
s: Add a row per employee once their UAN/ESI number is allotted.
Tick PF/ESI registered as each goes through; leave unticked while pending.
pf-esi-register.tip: This is the registration record, not the contribution calculation — percentages and the wage ceiling are set on PF & ESI.
pf-esi-register.why: A registration date and UAN per employee is what an inspector or a bank audit asks for first — keeping it as its own short record means it isn't buried inside the full employee profile.
pf-esi-register.uc: A new joiner's UAN comes through from EPFO three weeks after joining — add it here the day it arrives, without touching the employee's main record.
adv: One place to see who is/isn't registered yet
Simple audit-ready register

tds-declarations.g: Per-employee, per-year investment/exemption declaration for salary TDS
tds-declarations.w: A generic-module register of each employee's annual tax declaration: Employee, Financial year, Tax regime (Old/New), Declared investment/exemption amount, whether HR has verified it, and the verification date.
s: Add one row per employee per financial year when they submit their declaration.
Tick Verified once HR has checked the proofs, and record the date.
tds-declarations.tip: This is the declared figure only — it feeds how much is withheld under Sec 192, but the withholding itself happens in payroll, not on this screen.
tds-declarations.why: An employee's regime choice and declared exemptions have to be on record for the whole year, separately from any one month's payslip.
tds-declarations.uc: An employee switches to the old regime and declares an 80C investment — record it here once, and HR has it on file when payroll or the employee later asks what was declared.
adv: One record per employee per year
HR verification tracked, not just the number

bonus-register.w: A generic-module register for the Payment of Bonus Act: Employee, Financial year, bonus-eligible salary, bonus % and amount, the date paid, and a Pending/Paid status. Nothing here is calculated automatically — amounts are entered directly.
f: Status: Pending / Paid, with paid-on date
s: Add a row per employee once the year's bonus percentage is decided.
Mark Paid and set the date once disbursed.
bonus-register.tip: This is a record-keeping register, not a calculator — work out the eligible salary and percentage first, then enter the result here.
bonus-register.why: Statutory bonus is an annual, once-a-year obligation with its own filing/audit trail — worth its own register separate from the ad-hoc Bonus & Encashment entries used the rest of the year.
bonus-register.uc: Year-end: HR decides an 8.33% bonus for eligible staff, enters each employee's amount here, and marks each Paid as the payout goes out.
adv: Clean per-year audit trail
Separate from day-to-day bonus/encashment entries

min-wages.w: A generic-module reference list: State, Skill category (Unskilled / Semi-skilled / Skilled / Highly skilled), the minimum wage per month, and the date it took effect. Purely a reference table — nothing in payroll currently checks against it automatically.
s: Add a row whenever a state revises its minimum wage notification — State, Skill category, the new amount and its effective date.
Keep the old row rather than editing it in place, so the history of past rates for that state and category stays on record.
Use the Effective from date to answer “what was the minimum wage on this date” if a wage is ever questioned.
min-wages.tip: This is a reference table you maintain by hand — there's no automatic feed from government notifications, and no payroll check against it yet.
min-wages.why: Minimum wage revisions happen per state on no fixed schedule; keeping the current figure on record is what you show if a wage is ever questioned.
min-wages.uc: A state revises the unskilled minimum wage — add a new row with the new amount and effective date, keeping the old one for history.
adv: Simple, always-visible reference
One place instead of hunting old notifications

compliance.g: Declared expiry checks — DRA, PCC, bank authorisations, employee documents
compliance.w: Four checks declared in config/compliance.json each run against your data: DRA certification and Police Clearance Certificate (from the Employees screen), Bank authorisation letters (per agent/portfolio) and Employee documents (ID/address proofs etc). Each check is shown as its own card with four counts — Lapsed, Expiring soon, No date recorded, In date — and, unless everything is fine, a table of Who / State / Expiry / Days. What you see is scoped to you: an executive sees their own date, a manager their team's, HR everybody's; rows outside your scope are counted as hidden, not silently dropped from the total.
f: Four declared checks: DRA, PCC, bank authorisation, documents
Per-check counts: Lapsed / Expiring soon / No date recorded / In date
Findings table: Who, State, Expiry, Days
"Customise this check" link, for those who can change tenant settings
s: Open Compliance Watch and read each card's counts — Lapsed first, then Expiring soon.
"No date recorded" is not the same as compliant — it means nobody has entered a date yet; treat it as a gap to close.
Use "Customise this check" (if you have tenant.settings.update) to adjust a check's warning window.
compliance.tip: A row with no expiry date is reported as its own state, never folded into either 'in date' or 'expired' — so it can never hide inside a clean-looking count.
r: Everyone — sees only what their scope covers
Admin & HR — the full tenant view
compliance.rel: Also see: Off-roll Agents, Agent Authorization, Employees
compliance.why: A compliance screen that reports a date without saying what the date prevents is a list nobody acts on — every check here states in words what it blocks (allocation of recovery work, field visits, collection on a portfolio) so a lapsed row reads as a real consequence, not a housekeeping note.
compliance.uc: Picture this: the DRA card shows 2 lapsed and 3 expiring within 60 days. You renew the 2 lapsed immediately and start the 3 renewals early, so nobody is ever fielded on an expired credential.
adv: Four real obligations checked automatically from existing data — no separate register to maintain
Scoped counts mean a manager sees exactly their own exposure, not the whole tenant's
A blank date is flagged, never miscounted as 'fine'
mk: Reading a check as 'nothing to act on' because it shows zero lapsed
Zero lapsed can still hide a large 'no date recorded' count — that group has never been assessed at all
Check all four counts on every card, not just the lapsed number

salary-advance.g: Advance requests with a configured multi-level approval chain, tenure, and an EMI recovery schedule — not a plain register
salary-advance.w: Requesting and approving a salary advance: pick the employee (their manager, designation, department and branch auto-fill from the record), state a reason, an amount requested and an amount sanctioned. Below that, one dropdown per approval level declared in config/salary-advance.json — typically manager, director and HR admin — each with its own signer and status, so an advance is never approved by one person deciding alone. A tenure dropdown and a live EMI preview (mirroring the server's own rounding — sanctioned amount divided by tenure, rounded up to the rupee) let you see the recovery plan before saving, and an EMI-start-month picker sets when recovery begins. The table lists every advance with its full approval trail, tenure, EMI, EMI start, status, how much has been recovered so far and the balance remaining. "Disburse" moves a sanctioned advance to paid; a link to the Claims screen opens the approvals queue for whoever is next in the chain.
f: Employee picker auto-fills manager, designation, department and branch
Three configured approval levels (manager / director / HR admin), each with its own signer and status
Live EMI preview as you choose tenure — the same rounding the server uses when it saves
Recovered-so-far and balance columns, updated as EMIs are recovered through payroll
s: Pick the employee — their reporting details fill in automatically — then enter the reason and amounts.
Choose tenure and watch the EMI preview before saving, so the recovery plan is clear up front.
Move each approval level along in order; "Disburse" only becomes the next step once sanctioned.
Use "Approvals queue" (Claims) to see everything currently waiting on your own signature.
salary-advance.tip: The EMI preview you see while choosing tenure is not just a display convenience — it uses the exact same sanctioned÷tenure, rounded-up-to-the-rupee rule the server applies when it actually saves the EMI, so what you see is what gets recovered.
r: Whoever is named as the signer at each configured approval level
salary-advance.rel: Also see: Loans, Claim Approvals, Clawbacks / Reversals
salary-advance.why: An advance with no approval chain is one person's decision to lend company money against a future payslip. Three configured levels, each recorded with its own signer and status, means every advance carries who approved it and when — not just that it happened.
salary-advance.uc: Picture this: an employee requests ₹20,000 over 4 months. You sanction it, the manager and director approve, HR admin signs off, and the table now shows a ₹5,000 EMI starting next month — recovered automatically as payroll closes each period, with the balance visible the whole way through.
adv: Multi-level approval is configured, not hand-rolled per request — config/salary-advance.json decides how many levels and who signs
EMI recovery is computed the same way client-side and server-side, so nobody is surprised by a rounding difference
Recovered-so-far and balance are always visible, so an advance never becomes a number someone has to reconstruct from payslips
mk: Assuming this is a plain Add/Edit/Delete register, like a generic module screen
It is the same screen SmartPRS 2 relied on — approval levels, tenure, EMI and disbursement are all part of it, not optional extras
Use the approval-level dropdowns and Disburse action in order; don't look for a separate approvals screen for this specific flow

punch.g: The signed-in employee's own self-service punch — one button, direction decided automatically
punch.w: A self-service Punch In/Out for the account's own bound employee record, needing the ess.attendance.punch permission (granted to every role for this specific screen, since punching your own attendance isn't a privileged act). It reads today's open punches to decide the direction itself — the button reads "Punch IN" or "Punch OUT", never asking you to choose wrong — and shows First in, Last out, Worked so far and today's punch count. Pressing the button asks the browser for a location once; denied or slow, it still submits without one, and a geo-fence rule (if configured) judges the punch afterwards rather than blocking it up front. This is one of three ways a punch lands in the same register: this web screen, a biometric device, or a file punch import — all end up on the same per-employee Attendance record.
f: One button; direction (IN or OUT) is decided from today's open punches, not chosen by you
Location is requested once per punch; a denial or timeout still lets the punch through
First in / Last out / Worked so far / Punches, for today, at a glance
Lands in the same attendance register as device and file punches — not a separate log
s: Press the single button — it already knows whether this is an IN or an OUT.
Allow the location prompt if you can; if you can't or it's slow, the punch still goes through.
Check Today or your own Attendance screen afterwards if you want to confirm it landed.
punch.tip: An account with no employee bound to it (checked via the Accounts screen) has nobody to punch for — the screen says so plainly rather than letting you punch into nothing.
r: Every role — ess.attendance.punch is granted broadly, since this only ever touches the signed-in person's own record
punch.why: A self-punch that silently fails when GPS is denied trains people to distrust the button. Submitting without a location rather than blocking the punch — and letting a geo-fence rule judge it afterwards — means the record of when someone worked is never held hostage by whether their phone gave up a location.
punch.uc: Picture this: you arrive at your desk, press Punch IN, allow the location prompt, and by lunch the Attendance screen already shows your worked time so far — no device, no separate app, nothing for anyone else to enter on your behalf.
adv: One button that can't be pressed the wrong way — the direction is computed, not chosen
Works even when location is denied or slow, instead of blocking the punch entirely
Feeds the exact same register attendance reports and payroll already read — no reconciliation needed

general-settings.g: Every config/*.json rule file, whether this organisation has customised it, and where to actually change it
general-settings.w: SmartPRS 2's Settings was one form of switches; here every rule that can vary is its own config/*.json file, and "settings" is the inventory of those files — what each one declares, whether this tenant has customised it (with a version number, who changed it and when), or whether it's shipped as-is. Nothing is edited from this screen itself: each customisable file is changed on the screen that owns that rule (Configuration, a module's own Customise action, Probation Settings, Financial Year, and so on) — this is a map, not an editor. A short block above the table shows this organisation's own identity (name, code, timezone, currency, locale, status) as provisioned, not editable here either, since tenant identity is what every row in the database is scoped by.
f: Every config/*.json rule file the product ships, with a plain-language note on what it declares
Customised files show their version number and who last changed them, when
This organisation's own identity block: name, code, timezone, currency, locale, status
Links to Configuration (customisation history) and Menu, rather than an edit form here
s: Use this screen to see, at a glance, which rules this organisation has customised away from the shipped defaults.
Click through to Configuration for a customised file's version history.
To actually change a rule, go to the screen that owns it — this screen never writes a file itself.
general-settings.tip: A rule file with no customisation key listed is a product rule, changed only in the repository — it is intentionally not tenant-editable, not a gap in this screen.
general-settings.rel: Also see: Configuration, Menu, Probation Settings, Financial Year
general-settings.why: A single settings form that writes straight into the database hides who changed what and when. Listing every rule file's customisation status — version, changed-by, changed-at — and sending the actual edit to the screen that owns that rule keeps every change versioned and attributable (Law 3), instead of one shared form silently overwriting the last person's edit.
general-settings.uc: Picture this: payroll numbers look different this month and nobody remembers changing anything. You open General Settings, see the salary structure rule file is marked "customised v3, changed by Priya, 2 days ago", and now know exactly where to look and who to ask.
adv: One screen shows every customisable rule's status, without needing repository access to check
Every customisation carries a version and an author — nothing here is an anonymous edit
Tenant identity is shown but never editable here — it's provisioned, not a settings field

report-birthdays.g: One declared list report from the Reports Hub — upcoming birthdays, scoped to what you can see
report-birthdays.w: A single list report declared in config/field-reports.json, rendered by the same shared list-report partial every other Reports Hub report uses — this screen file itself is a 4-line wrapper (reportKey = 'birthdays') that hands off entirely to that shared engine. It reads DOB off the employee record and shows who has a birthday coming up, scoped to what the viewer's role can see (the same scope rules as everywhere else — an executive sees their own, a manager their team's, HR everyone's). Because it's declarative, adding another list report like this one is a config change, not a new PHP file.
f: Upcoming birthdays, read from each employee's DOB
Scoped the same way as every other list — rows outside your view are never shown
Declared once in config/field-reports.json, rendered by the shared list-report engine
s: Open Birthdays from Reports & Analytics to see who's coming up, within your own scope.
Use it alongside Greetings if you also want to queue a birthday message for someone on this list.
report-birthdays.tip: An employee with no DOB on record simply can't appear here — the same gap shows up on the Greetings screen, which is where it's worth fixing first.
r: Everyone — sees only what their scope covers
report-birthdays.why: A one-off "birthdays" screen that isn't built the same way as every other report would be one more place to fix when the scoping rule changes. Declaring it as one more row in the same list-report config means it inherits every fix made to the shared engine, forever, for free.
report-birthdays.uc: Picture this: HR wants a quick check of who has a birthday this month before planning office celebrations — this screen is exactly that list, already scoped so nobody sees birthdays outside their own view.
adv: Zero bespoke code — one declared key in config/field-reports.json is the entire screen
Automatically inherits scope rules and any future fix made to the shared list-report engine
Pairs directly with Greetings for anyone who wants to act on what they see here

claims.g: One approval queue for Expense Claims and Salary Advances — approve or reject with a reason, nothing decided silently
claims.w: Everything waiting on a decision across two registers — Expense Claims and Salary Advances — in one queue, scoped by Organization Setup. Approve or reject each with a reason (required to reject); the decision itself is written by a dedicated action, never here, and lands on the row (status, who, when) with the reason kept in the audit trail. A "Recently decided" panel below shows the last 20 decisions either way, so a decision is never invisible the moment it's made.
f: Expense claims and salary advances in one pending queue, not two
Approve or reject inline, with a reason required to reject
Recently decided panel — the last 20 decisions, either way
Direct links to the Expense Claims and Salary Advance registers themselves
s: Open Claim Approvals to see everything currently waiting on a decision, across both kinds.
Approve, or reject with a reason — the reason is required to reject, never optional.
Check Recently Decided if you need to confirm a decision already landed.
claims.tip: A claim raised by someone is never decided by the same action — raising and deciding are always two different, separately permissioned steps (payroll.view to raise, payroll.run to decide).
r: Approvers — payroll.run to decide; payroll.view to view the queue
claims.rel: Also see: Salary Advance, Expense Claims, Loans
claims.why: Two separate approval queues for two kinds of claim is two places to forget to check. One queue, with the kind badged on every row, means nothing waits unnoticed just because it's the less-visited of the two registers.
claims.uc: Picture this: an employee raises a ₹5,000 expense claim and another raises a salary advance the same week. Both show up here together — you approve one, reject the other with a reason — and both decisions are on record with who and when.
adv: One queue instead of two — nothing is missed because it's in "the other" register
A rejection always carries a reason, on the record, not just a status flip
Recently decided means a decision is confirmable without hunting through the source register

dra-certs.g: IIBF Debt Recovery Agent certificate status per employee, banded by days to expiry, recorded on the employee record itself
dra-certs.w: Every employee's DRA (Debt Recovery Agent) certificate status and expiry, banded against today: expiring within a configured window first, then expired, then valid, then not recorded. Nothing is entered here — the certificate is recorded on the Employees screen itself, and this screen reads it from there, so there is only one place a DRA date can ever live. A CSV export and the Organization Setup filter work the same way as every other field-operations report.
f: Expiring-first ordering, banded by a configurable window (expiry_window_days)
Reads the employee's own dra_status / dra_expiry — nothing duplicated here
CSV export, scoped by the Organization Setup filter
"Record" link jumps straight to the employee's own edit form
s: Open DRA Certificates and deal with anything expired or expiring within the window first.
Use "Record" on a row to jump straight to that employee's edit form — there's no separate entry form here.
Remember a certificate expiring today is already expired, not valid, on this screen.
dra-certs.tip: A certificate expiring today counts as expired, not valid — the question this screen answers is "does this agent hold a valid certificate today", and a same-day expiry answers no.
r: Everyone — employee.view, scoped to what they can see
dra-certs.rel: Also see: Compliance Watch, Agent Authorisations, Off-roll KYC & Earnings
dra-certs.why: A certificate register that's separate from the employee record is a second place for the date to go stale. Reading it live off the employee record means this screen can never show a date that the employee record itself doesn't also show.
dra-certs.uc: Picture this: three agents' DRA certificates expire within 30 days. You open this screen, see them banded as "due", and renew all three before any of them lapses — rather than finding out when a bank flags an unauthorised visit.
adv: One source of truth (the employee record) — nothing can drift out of sync with it
Expiring-first ordering means the most urgent renewals are always at the top
A same-day expiry is treated as expired, never miscounted as still valid

offroll-kyc.g: Per-agent KYC document checklist, contact/bank details, and a live earnings ledger priced automatically from their payout rate
offroll-kyc.w: For every off-roll (vendor) agent outside payroll: a KYC checklist against the declared document list (upload status per document, with a progress badge), editable contact/bank/UPI details, and a live earnings ledger for the picked month. Recording an earning (visits, amount collected, or an override) is priced automatically from the agent's own payout type and rate — per-visit, percent-of-collected, or fixed — by the same engine every time, and whoever records an entry is never the one who approves it. The bottom table lists every agent with their KYC completeness, DRA/PCC badges, and this month's approved total at a glance; the register of agents itself lives on the separate Off-roll Agents screen.
f: Per-agent KYC checklist against the declared document list, with an upload/replace action per document
Earnings priced automatically from the agent's own payout type and rate — never typed in free-hand
Record and approve are always two different people's actions
One summary table: every agent's KYC completeness, DRA/PCC status and this month's approved total
s: Pick an agent from the summary table to open their KYC and earnings for a month.
Upload or replace a document directly against its own row — no separate document manager.
Record an entry (visits or collected amount); someone else with payroll.run approves or rejects it before it counts toward the approved total.
offroll-kyc.tip: The amount field on a new entry is an override, not the default — leave it blank and the engine prices the entry itself from the agent's declared payout rate, which is the one source of truth for what an agent is owed.
r: employee.view to see this screen; employee.update to edit KYC/contact details; payroll.run to approve or reject an earning
offroll-kyc.rel: Also see: Off-roll Agents, Compliance Watch, Agent Authorisations
offroll-kyc.why: An off-roll agent isn't on payroll, so nothing about what they're owed can quietly happen inside a payroll run — this screen exists precisely because that money needs its own priced, approved, auditable trail outside it.
offroll-kyc.uc: Picture this: a field agent logs 12 visits this month at a per-visit rate. You record the entry, someone else approves it, and the approved total updates immediately — with the KYC documents that make the agent authorised to be in the field sitting right above it.
adv: Earnings are priced by the declared rate, never a manually typed amount someone has to double-check
Recording and approving are structurally two different actions — nobody can pay themselves
KYC completeness is visible at a glance across every agent, not buried in individual records

letters-nda.g: One declared letter kind from the shared letters engine — generate, track and re-download NDA / confidentiality letters
letters-nda.w: The NDA / Confidentiality letter, generated from the same shared letters engine every other HR letter uses (this screen file itself just sets kind='nda' and hands off) — pick an employee, generate the letter from the declared template, and it's tracked and re-downloadable from the same place every time. Adding a new letter kind elsewhere is a config change to the shared engine, not a new screen.
f: One declared kind ('nda') on the shared letters engine — no bespoke code for this letter
Generated letters are tracked and re-downloadable, not one-shot
Scoped to whoever the viewer's role can see, like every other employee-facing screen
s: Pick the employee and generate the NDA letter from the declared template.
Re-download a previously generated letter from the same screen — nothing needs regenerating to get a copy.
letters-nda.tip: Because this is one declared kind on a shared engine, a wording fix made to the letters engine or its template applies here immediately — there's no separate NDA-specific code to remember to update.
letters-nda.rel: Also see: Offer Letters, Warning Letters, Letter Templates
letters-nda.why: Six separate letter screens, each with their own copy of the generate/track/download logic, is six places the same bug could hide. One shared engine with six declared kinds means a fix made once is a fix made everywhere.
letters-nda.uc: Picture this: a new joiner needs an NDA signed before day one. You generate it here in seconds, and it's tracked the same way an offer letter would be — re-downloadable later if needed, with no separate filing step.
adv: Zero bespoke code for this specific letter — one declared kind on the shared engine
Every generated letter is tracked, so "was this ever sent" always has an answer
A template change in one place applies to this and every other letter kind together

asset-issue.g: Two sections, one screen: Asset Stock (what exists) and the Issue Tracker (who holds what) — every move stamped with who and when
asset-issue.w: What is on hand and what is issued to whom, in two sections on one screen per the owner's own instruction. Asset Stock is the register of what exists — add an item and it always starts "In stock"; correcting an asset's own facts (name, serial, cost) happens through its one edit form, reachable from the pencil icon, never a separate menu item. The Issue Tracker moves an asset through its declared transitions — issue, return, repair, retire — stamping who and when on every move, and now also records what a damaged or lost return recovers and whether that recovery has been settled. health.g: Real checks against real thresholds — a probe that throws counts as failing, never as a quiet green tick
health.w: Every installation health probe the platform runs, each with what was observed, its threshold, what to do about a failure, and whose job it is to act. A probe that throws an error is recorded as "unknown" and counted as failing — deliberately, because a monitoring screen that goes green when it can't actually reach the thing it's checking is worse than one that visibly fails. Nothing here is decorative: the platform refuses to register a check with no remediation step and no named owner, so every red row tells you what to do next, not just that something is wrong.
f: Every probe with observed value, threshold, and pass/fail/unknown state
A probe that throws is recorded as failing, never silently skipped
Every check declares its own remediation step and owner — no orphaned alerts
One overall badge: all clear, or how many are currently failing
s: Check the overall badge first — all clear, or a count of failing checks.
For anything failing, read its "what to do" column before escalating — the remediation step is stated, not left to guesswork.
An "unknown" status is not a lesser problem than a clear failure — treat it the same way.
health.tip: A check marked "unknown" means the probe itself couldn't run — that's treated as a failure, not a pass, because a monitor that silently can't reach what it's checking is the worst outcome a health screen can produce.
health.rel: Also see: General Settings, Statutory Configuration, Activity Logs
health.why: A health check with no stated remediation and no named owner is a notification that trains people to ignore notifications. Requiring both on every declared check means a red row is always actionable, never just noise.
health.uc: Picture this: a check for disk space turns red. The row already states the threshold it crossed, what to do about it, and whose job that is — no separate runbook to find.
adv: A probe that errors counts as failing, never as a false-positive green
Every check carries its own remediation and owner — nothing here is just informational noise
One badge gives the whole-system answer before you need to read a single row

api-keys.g: Scoped credentials, shown once at creation and never again — stored only as a hash, revoked meaningfully because no copy exists to keep using
api-keys.w: Every API credential issued for this tenant, each carrying scopes (a coarser, statable vocabulary than the full permission catalogue — "this key can read employees" is a sentence someone issuing it can actually weigh) rather than a role. A newly minted token is shown exactly once, immediately after creation, then dropped from the session before anything else can go wrong — it is stored only as a hash and cannot be recovered by anyone, ever, which is what makes a revoke meaningful: there is no copy anywhere for someone to keep using after it's revoked. Every list row shows name, prefix, scopes, expiry and last-used time; an endpoint whose scope a credential doesn't hold is refused even when the underlying code path would otherwise have worked.
f: Issue a scoped credential; the raw token is shown exactly once, at creation
Stored only as a hash — not recoverable by you, support, or anyone reading the database
last_used_at stamped on every authenticated request, so an unused key is identifiable
Revoke is meaningful: there is no surviving copy of the token anywhere to keep using
s: Issue a credential with the narrowest scope that does the job — not a blanket one "to be safe".
Copy the shown token immediately; it will never be displayed again after this screen.
Check last_used_at periodically and revoke anything that's gone quiet.
api-keys.tip: The minted token shown after creation is the only time it will ever appear — if it's lost before it's copied, the only recovery is to revoke that credential and mint a new one; there is no "show it again" option, by design.
r: access.apikey.list to view; access.apikey.issue to mint a new credential
api-keys.rel: Also see: Activity Logs, Roles & Permissions
api-keys.why: A token stored in a way that lets anyone recover it later is a token that can be silently copied and reused by anyone who can read the database. Storing only a hash means a revoke is absolute — there is no lingering copy for the same secret to keep working elsewhere.
api-keys.uc: Picture this: an integration key hasn't been used since March. You check last_used_at, confirm it's genuinely stale, and revoke it — knowing that revoke actually ends every use of that token, because no copy of it exists to keep going.
adv: Scopes are a sentence a person can weigh, not an opaque role name
A hash-only store makes every revoke absolute — nothing can keep using a revoked token
last_used_at turns "is this key still needed" into an answerable question, not a guess

kra-kpi.g: Which KPIs from the industry catalogue apply where, and their targets — scoped by company/branch/role, dated, never overwritten
kra-kpi.w: The Key Result Area / Key Performance Indicator catalogue — seeded from the collections/recovery industry's own KRA/KPI matrix — configured per scope (company, branch, or role; a blank dropdown means All). For each scope you tick "Keep" on every KPI that should count there, and enter a target for whichever already has one agreed; a KPI can be kept with no target yet. Only kept KPIs show up on KPI Achievements for an employee in that scope, and the most specific scope covering an employee always wins (role beats branch beats tenant-wide). Saving never overwrites a target: it closes whatever was open for that exact scope and opens new, dated rows for what's currently ticked, so an achievement recorded last month stays explained by last month's target even after this month's setting changes. A handful of KPIs are marked as having a companion figure — the matrix itself defines an achievement KPI recorded elsewhere against this target, plus a percentage worked out automatically from the two — so that companion and percentage never appear here as something to separately target.
f: Scope by company, branch or role — a blank dropdown means All
Keep/target each KPI independently — a KPI can be kept with no target yet
Saving opens new dated rows rather than overwriting — old achievements stay explained by their own target
A companion-KPI badge marks pairs where the achievement and its ratio are computed elsewhere, never targeted here
s: Pick the scope (company/branch/role) this set of targets applies to — leave blank for All.
Tick Keep on every KPI relevant to that scope, and fill in a target for whichever is already agreed.
Save — this closes the old set for that exact scope and opens a new, dated one; nothing already recorded against the old target changes.
kra-kpi.tip: The most specific scope covering an employee always wins — a role-scoped setting beats a branch-scoped one, which beats a tenant-wide one, so a role-specific target doesn't need to also be repeated at the branch or tenant level.
