kra-kpi.why: A single flat KPI catalogue with no scoping would force every branch and role onto the same targets regardless of relevance. Scoping with a most-specific-wins rule, and never overwriting a target once achievements exist against it, means history stays explained even as policy evolves.
kra-kpi.uc: Picture this: field collection KPIs matter for one branch's role but not another's. Scope the Keep/target set to that role, and only employees in it see those KPIs on their own KPI Achievements — nobody else is offered a target that doesn't apply to them.
adv: Scoped, most-specific-wins targeting — not one flat catalogue for every role and branch
A target is never overwritten — past achievements always stay explained by the target that was actually in force then
Computed companion figures (an achievement and its ratio) are never duplicated as something to separately target

configure-id-card.g: Named, scoped ID card formats — company/branch/department/role/designation/employee — previewed against a real employee where one is in scope
configure-id-card.w: Design and preview the ID card layout, with named format entries each scoped to a combination of company, branch, department, role, designation, or a single employee — editing an entry loads its saved format back into the same form. The preview uses a real employee from your scope where one exists, never a customer's actual name typed into a sample; where an entry is scoped to a template sentinel rather than a real person, the preview shows that template's own placeholder instead of whichever real employee happened to sort first, so a name never appears on a badge preview it shouldn't.
f: Named, scoped format entries — not one global layout for every card
Scope by company, branch, department, role, designation, or a single employee
Live preview against a real in-scope employee, or a plainly-labelled sample when none applies
Editing an entry loads its saved format straight back into the design form
s: Create a named format entry and scope it to whichever level needs its own card design.
Use the live preview to check the layout before saving — it reflects a real employee wherever your scope allows one.
Edit an existing entry to load its format back in, rather than starting a new one from scratch.
configure-id-card.tip: A more specific scope (say, one designation) doesn't need to duplicate a broader entry's whole design — create it only where the design actually needs to differ.
r: tenant.settings.view; tenant.settings.update to change a format
configure-id-card.rel: Also see: ID Cards, Organization Setup
configure-id-card.why: One global ID card design forces every department and designation onto the same layout even when a client legitimately needs different cards for different roles. Named, scoped entries mean each one is designed once and previewed honestly, without ever putting a real name on a template that isn't theirs.
configure-id-card.uc: Picture this: field agents need a card with different fields than office staff. Create a format entry scoped to the field role, design it, preview it against a real field employee, and office staff keep using the broader entry untouched.
adv: Multiple card designs by scope, not one design forced on everyone
Preview always uses a real employee where possible — never a placeholder pretending to be one
Editing loads the exact saved format back — no redesigning from a blank form each time

leave-absence.g: Leave types, eligibility, grants, and unauthorized-absence escalation — one screen, per the owner's own instruction, not two to click between
leave-absence.w: Leave Types (which leaves this company gives, how many days, whether they carry forward, and — after Note — who they even apply to) and Grants (by company, branch, department, designation, team or employee, landing on the actual leave ledgers) sit together with Unauthorized Absence escalation on one screen, deliberately — the owner asked for one place rather than two menu items to click between. Leave types default to the shipped list until saved once, after which they become this company's own versioned list; blank rows in the editor are ignored, and clearing a type's code and name is how you remove it. A type that doesn't carry forward lapses automatically at year end. Company, Branch, Role and Designation, after Note, narrow which employees a type is even offered to — leave all four on ALL for a type everyone can use; name one or more and only a matching employee sees the type, can be granted it, or can request it, in requests and in grants alike. Maternity and Paternity Leave carry one further, fixed restriction that isn't a column here because it never varies by tenant: they apply only to employees whose Marital Status (set in the Employee Directory) is Married.
f: Leave Types: code, name, paid/unpaid, opening days, monthly accrual, maximum, carry-forward, encashable
Eligibility columns after Note — Company, Branch, Role, Designation — narrow who a type applies to; Maternity/Paternity are additionally fixed to Married employees only
Grants scoped by company, branch, department, designation, team or individual employee — and still bounded by the type's own eligibility above
Unauthorized Absence: a run of consecutive unexplained absence, not a single day, escalating through configurable day-thresholds
Shipped defaults until saved once; every save after that is this company's own versioned list
s: Edit the Leave Types table — blank rows are ignored, clear a row's code and name to remove that type.
Set Company / Branch / Role / Designation after Note only for a type that shouldn't be offered to everyone — leave them on ALL otherwise.

Use Grants to land specific leave allocations on the ledgers for a scope narrower than the type's own default; an employee outside the type's own eligibility is skipped even if the grant's scope would otherwise reach them.

Under Unauthorized Absence, set the day count for Abscond, First Warning, Second Warning and Final Full & Final, and who is always cc'd, then use "Evaluate the day" / "Run now" to sweep and see the results in the Log below rather than waiting for the next scheduled pass.
leave-absence.tip: Abscond is a RUN, not a day: a weekly-off or holiday inside a run of unexplained absence neither counts toward it nor breaks it, but a real punch or an approved leave ends it outright — so a long weekend inside an absence doesn't quietly reset the clock, and a single day back at work does. "Evaluate the day" reports every crossing even with escalation switched off; it just tells nobody about them in that case.
r: Whichever permission each section requires — tenant.settings.update to change types, eligibility, or the escalation configuration
leave-absence.rel: Also see: Leave, Holiday / W.OFF Schedule, Employee Directory (Marital Status)
leave-absence.why: Splitting leave types, their eligibility, grants and unauthorized-absence escalation across separate screens would scatter one coherent HR policy area across menu items that don't obviously relate. Keeping them together means changing leave policy, who it applies to, and its escalation is one visit, not four.
leave-absence.uc: Picture this: a new leave type needs adding company-wide, plus a specific grant for one department that gets extra days, plus a rule that a type is only for one branch's staff — all three happen on this one screen. Separately, an employee who hasn't shown up in days and hasn't been heard from starts a run the Unauthorized Absence section is already watching, and it notifies the same people the owner configured — Company Admin, Branch Admin, HR Admin and HR Manager by default, preferring whoever holds that role in the absent employee's own company — without anyone having to notice the absence themselves first.
adv: One screen for a policy area that genuinely belongs together, not four unrelated-looking menu items
Leave types, their eligibility and the escalation rules are all versioned like every other tenant customisation — a policy change is dated, never an untracked overwrite
A type that shouldn't carry forward lapses on its own — nobody has to remember to zero it out

Maternity/Paternity eligibility and any Company/Branch/Role/Designation restriction are enforced wherever the type is used — on the balance shown to the employee, on a self-service request, and on a grant — not just hidden from one screen

biometric-config.g: Provider, endpoint and enabled/disabled per biometric integration — a plain configuration register
biometric-config.w: A plain Add/Edit/Delete register of biometric integration configurations — label, provider, base URL, endpoint, whether it's enabled, and when it last synced. This is the configuration side (which providers are wired up and where they point); the devices themselves are registered on the separate Biometric Devices module, and a ZKTeco device specifically has its own operational view (push URL, last punch, troubleshooting) on ZKTeco Devices.
f: Provider, base URL and endpoint per biometric integration
Enable or disable an integration without deleting its configuration
Last synced timestamp per configured integration
s: Add a configuration row per biometric provider you integrate with.
Disable rather than delete a configuration you're not currently using — the settings stay for when you need them again.
biometric-config.tip: This is the integration configuration, not the device register itself — look at Biometric Devices for the actual devices, and ZKTeco Devices for that brand's own push-URL and troubleshooting view.
biometric-config.rel: Also see: Biometric Devices, ZKTeco Devices, API Keys
biometric-config.why: Keeping integration configuration (provider, endpoint, enabled state) separate from the device register itself means disabling a provider doesn't require deleting every device registered against it.
biometric-config.uc: Picture this: you're evaluating a second biometric provider without disconnecting the first. Add its configuration here, enabled, alongside the existing one — nothing about the first provider's setup is disturbed.
adv: Disabling an integration is reversible — its configuration isn't lost
Separate from the device register, so provider-level and device-level changes don't collide

messages-log.g: Every message actually sent — target, recipients, channels, content, and who sent it — the audit trail for outbound communication
messages-log.w: A plain register of every message this tenant has sent — when, to what target, through which channels, the message content itself, and who sent it. This is the log, not a compose screen: Send Message, Notice Board and Greetings are where a message originates; every one of them lands here, so there's a single place to confirm what actually went out, to whom, and when.
f: Every sent message: when, target, recipients, channels, content, sender
The landing place for everything sent from Send Message, Notice Board and Greetings
s: Check this log to confirm a message actually went out, rather than trusting that a compose screen's submit succeeded.
Use it to see exactly what content was sent to a given target, word for word.
messages-log.tip: This screen never composes or sends anything itself — it's purely the record of what already went out from elsewhere.
messages-log.rel: Also see: Send Message, Notice Board, Greetings
messages-log.why: Sending a message from three different screens (Send Message, Notice Board, Greetings) without one shared log would mean confirming delivery requires checking three different places. One log for all of them means "was this sent" always has one answer, regardless of where it originated.
messages-log.uc: Picture this: someone asks whether a notice actually reached a branch last week. Check this log — target, channel and content are all there, regardless of which of the three compose screens sent it.
adv: One log for messages from every compose screen — nowhere else to check
Exact content sent is recorded, not just a "sent" flag

complaints.g: A plain complaint register — channel, severity, status through a declared workflow, per employee
complaints.w: A plain Add/Edit/Delete register for complaints against field staff: channel (WhatsApp, SMS, email, push, in-app), the employee it concerns, date, source, severity, and a status that moves through a declared workflow — Received, Under review, Substantiated, Unsubstantiated, Closed — plus a free-text description. This is a straightforward register, not a confidentiality-scoped one: unlike POSH Complaints, there's no special visibility restriction here beyond the ordinary employee.view permission.
f: Channel, employee, date, source, severity and status per complaint
Status moves through a declared workflow: Received → Under review → Substantiated/Unsubstantiated → Closed
Free-text description field for the full detail
s: Log a complaint with its channel and severity as soon as it's received.
Move its status along the declared workflow as it's investigated, ending at Substantiated, Unsubstantiated or Closed.
complaints.tip: This register has no special confidentiality scoping — anyone with employee.view can see every complaint here, unlike POSH Complaints, which is deliberately kept out of the ordinary module engine for exactly that reason.
complaints.rel: Also see: Off-roll Agents, Off-roll KYC & Earnings, POSH Complaints
complaints.why: A declared status workflow (rather than free-text status) means a complaint can't be marked with a status that doesn't exist, and every complaint's progress is comparable against every other's.
complaints.uc: Picture this: a customer complaint comes in via WhatsApp about a field agent. Log it here with its channel and severity, move it to Under review while it's investigated, and close it out with a final Substantiated or Unsubstantiated status.
adv: A fixed, declared status workflow — no free-text status that means something different every time
Every field for a complaint (channel, severity, source) is structured, not buried in a single note

smtp-settings.g: Not built — no table, no screen, in this build; still hidden in the sidebar for that reason
smtp-settings.w: There is no Email / SMTP Settings screen, table, or configuration path anywhere in this build — this key describes that gap honestly rather than pretending a generic register covers it. General Settings (which this item might be mistaken for) is a rule-file inventory screen, not SMTP configuration, and no smtp_settings-style table exists in any migration. Adding a plausible-looking generic module on top of a table that doesn't exist would make the sidebar item look fixed while the screen actually errors the moment it's opened — so this stays a genuine, flagged gap rather than a config patch. Building it for real needs a migration (under database/migrations, run offline, never at request time — Law 2) plus a dedicated screen for host/port/encryption/credentials.
f: No table, no screen — genuinely not built, not merely hidden by mistake
s: Don't look for SMTP configuration on General Settings — that screen is a different thing (a rule-file inventory).
Raise this with whoever owns the build backlog if outbound email needs configuring — it needs a real migration and screen, not a config change.
smtp-settings.tip: This is one of a small number of nav items left intentionally hidden because building a fake module on top of a non-existent table would look fixed while actually breaking the moment someone opens it.
r: Would be tenant.settings.view / tenant.settings.update once built
smtp-settings.rel: Also see: General Settings, SMS Settings
smtp-settings.why: A module definition pointed at a table that was never migrated doesn't fix a broken menu item — it just moves the failure from "hidden" to "errors on open". Naming the gap here, honestly, is more useful than a green checkmark that isn't true.
smtp-settings.uc: Picture this: someone wants payslip email notifications configured. This screen doesn't exist yet to do that — the request needs a real migration and screen built, not a setting flipped somewhere.
adv: Documented honestly as unbuilt, so nobody wastes time hunting for a setting that doesn't exist
